Periodic Points in Genus Two: Holomorphic Sections over Hilbert Modular Varieties, Teichmüller dynamics, and Billiards

Paul Apisa
Abstract.

We show that all GL⁡(2,ℝ)\GL(2,\mathbb{R}) equivariant point markings over orbit closures of primitive genus two translation surfaces arise from marking pairs of points exchanged by the hyperelliptic involution, Weierstrass points, or the golden points on Ω​E5\Omega E_{5}. As corollaries, we classify the holomorphically varying families of points over orbifold covers of genus two Hilbert modular surfaces, solve the finite blocking problem on genus two translation surfaces, and show that there is at most one nonarithmetic rank two orbit closure in ℋ⁡(6)\mathcal{H}(6).

1. Introduction

The bundle of holomorphic one-forms over the moduli space of Riemann surfaces admits a GL⁡(2,ℝ)\GL(2,\mathbb{R}) action arising from its complex structure and Teichmüller geodesic flow. While the goal of classifying every GL⁡(2,ℝ)\GL(2,\mathbb{R}) orbit closure is elusive in general, McMullen discovered a solution in genus two. In a sequence of papers [McM03], [McM05], [McM06], and [McM07], he showed that every orbit closure is one of the following: a stratum, a locus of torus covers, or a locus of eigenforms of real multiplication by an order in a real quadratic field.

Given a translation surface (X,ω)(X,\omega) a point pp is said to be a periodic point if pp is not a zero of ω\omega and (X,ω)(X,\omega) and (X,ω,p)(X,\omega;p) have orbit closures of the same dimension (that the orbit closures are manifolds and hence have a well-defined dimension follows from work of Eskin-Mirzakhani [EM] and Eskin-Mirzakhani-Mohammadi [EMM15]). A translation surface (X,ω)(X,\omega) is said to be primitive if ω\omega is not the pullback of a holomorphic one-form on a lower genus Riemann surface under a holomorphic branched cover. Möller [Möl06] showed that the only periodic points on primitive Veech surfaces in genus two are Weierstrass points. In Apisa [Apia], the author showed that the same holds for any genus two translation surface with dense orbit.

From these data one might be tempted to conjecture that Weierstrass points are the only possible periodic points on primitive genus two translation surfaces. However, Wright discovered two points - dubbed the golden points - on the golden eigenform locus that he conjectured were periodic. This conjecture was confirmed in Kumar-Mukamel [KM16] and will be re-established by different means in forthcoming work of Eskin-McMullen-Mukamel-Wright. We show the following:

Theorem 1.

If a primitive genus two translation surface contains a periodic point that is not a Weierstrass point then its orbit closure is the golden eigenform locus and the periodic point is one of the golden points.

The strategy of the proof is to reduce the problem to Möller’s classification of periodic points on primitive genus two Veech surfaces [Möl06] using degeneration arguments and the Mirzakhani-Wright partial compactification of an affine invariant submanifold [MW17]. The argument is presented in Section 2.

In fact, Theorem 1 implies a stronger result. Say that a collection of points BB on a translation surface (X,ω)(X,\omega) is generic if the complex dimension of the orbit closure of (X,ω,B)(X,\omega;B) is |B||B| more than the dimension of the orbit closure of (X,ω)(X,\omega). A collection of points will be called nongeneric otherwise.

Corollary 1.

Any nongeneric collection of points on a primitive genus two translation surface must contain singularities of the flat metric, periodic points (i.e. Weierstrass points or golden points), or two points exchanged by the hyperelliptic involution.

Proof of Corollary 1 assuming Theorem 1:

By Apisa-Wright [AW17, Theorem 1.3] any nongeneric collection of points on a translation surface (X,ω)(X,\omega) that does not contain a singularity or a periodic point must contain two points pp and qq that are identified under a holomorphic map f:X⟶Yf:X\longrightarrow Y where YY is a lower genus Riemann surface with an abelian or quadratic differential that pulls back to the flat structure on (X,ω)(X,\omega). Moreover, if this map does not factor through a map to a translation surface it is degree two. Since (X,ω)(X,\omega) is primitive it is not a torus cover so ff must be a degree two map to the sphere. Therefore, ff is the quotient by the hyperelliptic involution. ∎

As one application of the Theorem 1, we classify the nonarithmetic rank two affine invariant submanifolds in ℋ⁡(6)\mathcal{H}(6), using degenerations to find genus two nonarithmetic eigenforms with marked points in the boundary.

Theorem 2.

There is at most one nonarithmetic rank two orbit closure in ℋ⁡(6)\mathcal{H}(6). It has no periodic points.

The definition of the orbit closure and the proof of Theorem 2 will be given in Section 7. This orbit closure will be shown to be a rank two nonarithmetic affine invariant submanifold in forthcoming work of Eskin-McMullen-Mukamel-Wright.

As another application of Theorem 1 we compute holomorphic sections of the universal curve restricted to genus two Hilbert modular varieties.

The locus of principally polarized abelian varieties with real multiplication by an order in a totally real number field - or Hilbert modular variety - has an explicit description as the quotient of gg copies of the hyperbolic plane by a lattice (for details see van der Geer [vdG88]). Let XDX_{D} be the locus of abelian surfaces with real multiplication by the order 𝒪D=ℤ⁡[x]/(x2+b​x+c)\mathcal{O}_{D}=\mathbb{Z}[x]/(x^{2}+bx+c) where b2−4​c=Db^{2}-4c=D. Let EDE_{D} be the collection of Riemann surfaces whose Jacobian belong to XDX_{D} and let Ω​ED\Omega E_{D} be the collection of abelian differentials that are 𝒪D\mathcal{O}_{D}-eigenforms on a surface in EDE_{D}. The golden eigenform locus is defined to be the intersection of Ω​E5\Omega E_{5} and ℋ⁡(1,1)\mathcal{H}(1,1).

For any Riemann surface in EDE_{D} there are two holomorphic one-forms that are eigenforms of real-multiplication. The collection of (at most four) points where some eigenform vanishes forms a holomorphically varying family of points over EDE_{D}. Another such collection is the set of Weierstrass points. The question we take up here is whether there are any other such families of points.

Given a finite index subgroup of the mapping class group, let ED​(Γ)E_{D}(\Gamma) be the preimage of EDE_{D} under the finite orbifold cover of moduli space prescribed by Γ\Gamma. If Γ\Gamma is torsion free, then the universal curve on the cover restricts to a holomorphic surface bundle π:CD​(Γ)⟶ED​(Γ)\pi:C_{D}(\Gamma)\longrightarrow E_{D}(\Gamma). We will assume in the sequel that DD is not a perfect square.

Theorem 3.

Let Γ\Gamma be a torsionfree finite index subgroup of the mapping class group. There is a holomorphic section of π\pi over some component of ED​(Γ)E_{D}(\Gamma) that does not exclusively mark zeros of the eigenforms or Weierstrass points only if D=5D=5.

Proof of Theorem 3 given Theorem 1.

: Suppose that π\pi admits a section over a component of ED​(Γ)E_{D}(\Gamma) and let XX be a Riemann surface in that component. Let ω\omega be an 𝒪D\mathcal{O}_{D}-eigenform on XX. By Apisa [Apia] holomorphic sections of CD​(Γ)⟶ED​(Γ)C_{D}(\Gamma)\longrightarrow E_{D}(\Gamma) must mark periodic points or zeros of (X,ω)(X,\omega). By Theorem 1, periodic points that are not Weierstrass points only exist if D=5D=5 and the points are the golden points. ∎

Finally, we will show that Theorem 1 resolves the genus two finite blocking problem. Given a translation surface (X,ω)(X,\omega) and two points pp and qq (that are not necessarily distinct and that may coincide with zeros of ω\omega) the finite blocking problem asks whether there is a finite collection of points BB on (X,ω)−{p,q}(X,\omega)-\{p,q\} so that all straight lines between pp and qq must pass through BB. The analogous problem on a polygon TT is whether given two point pp and qq there is a finite collection of points BB in T−{p,q}T-\{p,q\} so that all billiard shots from pp to qq pass through BB. By unfolding the table TT to an abelian differential (X,ω)(X,\omega) and letting PP and QQ be the preimages of pp and qq respectively, the finite blocking problem in polygonal biliards reduces to the question of whether all points in PP are finitely blocked from all points in QQ on (X,ω)(X,\omega).

Lelièvre, Monteil, and Weiss [LMW16] showed that classifying invariant measures in ℋ⁡(2,02)\mathcal{H}(2,0^{2}) and ℋ⁡(1,1,02)\mathcal{H}(1,1,0^{2}) is related to solving the finite blocking problem. Such a classification is equivalent to Corollary 1 and yields the following:

Theorem 4.

A singular point on a primitive genus two translation surface is finitely blocked from no other point and a nonsingular point is only finitely blocked from its image under the hyperelliptic involution (and the blocking set is a subset of the collection of Weierstrass points).

Note that Lelièvre, Monteil, and Weiss [LMW16, Theorem 2] implies that for any point pp on a primitive genus two translation surface, pp is finitely blocked from only finitely many points. Theorem 4 determines exactly what that finite set is, i.e. empty if pp is a zero and a singleton containing the image of pp under the hyperelliptic involution otherwise. The strategy of this proof, which appears in Section 3, is to use the ideas of Lelièvre, Monteil, and Weiss [LMW16] alluded to above along with constraints on the geometry of eigenforms coming from McMullen’s prototype surfaces in [McM05] and work of Lelièvre and Weiss [LW15] on convex representations of eigenforms.

To apply Theorem 4 to polygons, we devise the following criterion:

Theorem 5.

A holomorphic kk-differential on the sphere canonically unfolds to a hyperelliptic abelian differential only if one of the following two conditions holds:

  1. (1)

    All but at most two of the singularities have cone angle an integer multiple of π2\frac{\pi}{2}

  2. (2)

    The cone angles of the singularities, listed with multiplicity, are either (a,a,b,b)​2​π\left(a,a,b,b\right)2\pi or (a,a,b)​2​π\left(a,a,b\right)2\pi where aa and bb are rational.

Theorem 5 is proved in Section 4 and necessary and sufficient conditions for the converse to hold are also established.

Given θ\theta, ℳ⁡(θ)\mathcal{M}(\theta) is the GL⁡(2,ℝ)\GL(2,\mathbb{R}) orbit closure of the unfolding of the generic polygon with rational angles θ\theta. Theorem 5 is used to construct a complete list of the billiard tables that unfold to genus two translation surfaces, and, along with Theorem 4, produces a solution to the finite blocking problem for these polygons (see Theorem 6, which is proved in Section 5).

Theorem 6.

The complete list of rational kk-gons that unfold to genus two translation surfaces is given in Figure 1.

  1. (1)

    For k=6k=6, the surface is a torus cover if and only if x1x2\frac{x_{1}}{x_{2}} and y1y2\frac{y_{1}}{y_{2}} are rational.

  2. (2)

    For k=4k=4, the surface is a torus cover if and only if x1x2\frac{x_{1}}{x_{2}} is rational.

  3. (3)

    For k=3k=3, only the (16,16,23)​π\left(\frac{1}{6},\frac{1}{6},\frac{2}{3}\right)\pi triangle unfolds to a torus cover.

The solution to the finite blocking problem on the kk-gons that do not unfold to torus covers is the following

  1. (1)

    For k=6k=6, the circled vertices are blocked from themselves.

  2. (2)

    For k≠6k\neq 6, if the figure has two circled vertices they are finitely blocked from each other by the solid points (which are midpoints of the faces or edges they are drawn on).

  3. (3)

    For k≠6k\neq 6, if the figure has one circled vertex it is blocked from itself except for θ=(13,23,12,12,12)​π\theta=\left(\frac{1}{3},\frac{2}{3},\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}\right)\pi, which has no pairs of finitely blocked points. The solid points form a blocking set.

  4. (4)

    In all other cases, there are no pairs of finitely blocked points.

Notice that for rational polygons that unfold to torus covers any two points are finitely blocked from each other. Therefore, Theorem 6 solves the finite blocking problem for rational polygons that unfold to genus two translation surfaces.

2. Proof of Theorem 1 - Periodic Points in Genus Two

Theorem 1 has been established by Möller [Möl06] in the case of Teichmüller curves in genus two and by the author [Apia] for strata of genus two abelian differentials. It remains to classify periodic points on nonarithmetic eigenform loci in ℋ⁡(1,1)\mathcal{H}(1,1).

Assumption 2.1.

ℳ\mathcal{M} is a nonarithmetic eigenform locus in ℋ⁡(1,1)\mathcal{H}(1,1).

In every nonarithmetic eigenform locus ℋ⁡(1,1)\mathcal{H}(1,1) there is a translation surface with three horizontal cylinders (this follows from Wright [Wri15, Theorem 1.10] by letting (X,ω)(X,\omega) be a translation surface in ℳ\mathcal{M} where the twist space coincides with the cylinder preserving space in the horizontal direction; it is also implicit in the work of McMullen [McM07, Section 7]). The horizontal cylinders will be glued together as in Figure 2. The specific horizontally and vertically periodic translation surface in Figure 2 with the lengths of the horizontal and vertical saddle connections labelled as in the figure will be called the golden tetromino. We will let ϕ\phi denote the golden ratio and ζ\zeta a vertical saddle connection contained in the topmost cylinder.

Assumption 2.2.

Fix a horizontally periodic translation surface (X,ω)(X,\omega) with dense GL⁡(2,ℝ)\GL(2,\mathbb{R}) orbit in ℳ\mathcal{M}. Suppose that the horizontal cylinders are connected as in Figure 2. Suppose too that pp is a periodic point that is not a Weierstrass point on (X,ω)(X,\omega). Let ℳ′\mathcal{M}^{\prime} be the orbit closure of (X,ω,p)(X,\omega;p) in ℋ⁡(1,1,0)\mathcal{H}(1,1,0).

Our goal is to show that ℳ\mathcal{M} is the golden eigenform locus and that pp is one of the two golden points (which will be defined shortly).

Label the horizontal cylinders of (X,ω)(X,\omega) from top to bottom as C1C_{1}, C2C_{2}, and C3C_{3}. The relative deformation that only alters the imaginary parts of periods is ρ=−i⁡(γ1∗−γ2∗+γ3∗)\rho=-i\left(\gamma_{1}^{*}-\gamma_{2}^{*}+\gamma_{3}^{*}\right) where γi\gamma_{i} is the core curve of CiC_{i} traveling left to right. Let t​ρ⋅(X,ω)t\rho\cdot(X,\omega) be the time tt flow along ρ\rho applied to (X,ω)(X,\omega) (see Figure 3). This will be called the ρ\rho-flow or the ρ\rho-orbit of (X,ω)(X,\omega). The portion of the ρ\rho-flow when tt is positive will be called the forward ρ\rho flow and, when tt is negative, the backward (or reverse) ρ\rho flow.

Assumption 2.3.

Suppose without loss of generality, perhaps after rotating by π\pi, that the topmost cylinder in (X,ω)(X,\omega) is shorter than the bottomost. Suppose too that (X,ω)(X,\omega) has been sheared so that the topmost cylinder contains a vertical saddle connection ζ\zeta. In the case that ℳ\mathcal{M} is the golden eigenform locus we will make the additional assumption that (X,ω)(X,\omega) is some surface on the ρ\rho orbit of the golden tetromino.

Since the tangent spaces of ℳ′\mathcal{M}^{\prime} and ℳ\mathcal{M} are isomorphic under the forgetful map we will let, with some abuse of notation, ρ\rho also denote the lift of ρ\rho to ℳ′\mathcal{M}^{\prime}.

Proposition 2.4.

Let (Y,η,q)(Y,\eta;q) be any genus two translation surface in the Mirzakhani-Wright partial compactification of ℳ′\mathcal{M}^{\prime}. The point qq coincides with a Weierstrass point or zero of η\eta if and only if (Y,η)(Y,\eta) lies on the boundary of ℳ\mathcal{M} or is contained in a Teichmüller curve in ℳ\mathcal{M}.

Proof.

By Mirzakhani-Wright [MW17, Theorem 1.1], if two periodic points (or a periodic point and a zero) coincide they do so along a proper affine invariant submanifold in ℳ\mathcal{M}. Since ℳ\mathcal{M} is three-dimensional, this must be either a Teichmüller curve in ℳ\mathcal{M} or in its boundary.

For the reverse direction, if (Y,η)(Y,\eta) is a genus two translation surface lying in a Teichmüller curve in the Mirzakhani-Wright partial compactification of ℳ\mathcal{M}, then either it is an eigenform locus in ℋ⁡(2)\mathcal{H}(2) or it is the decagon locus in ℋ⁡(1,1)\mathcal{H}(1,1). Möller [Möl06] showed that the only periodic points in these loci are Weierstrass points. By Mirzakhani-Wright [MW17, Theorem 1.1], the restriction of ℳ′\mathcal{M}^{\prime} to any Teichmüller curves it contains will be a periodic point or zero on the translation surfaces in those Teichmüller curves. ∎

Corollary 2.5.

If ℳ′\mathcal{M}^{\prime} contains a translation surface (Y,η,q)(Y,\eta;q) where qq is a Weierstrass point, then ℳ\mathcal{M} is the golden eigenform locus.

Proof.

By Proposition 2.4, (Y,η)(Y,\eta) must lie on a Teichmüller curve contained in ℳ\mathcal{M}. The only eigenform locus containing a Teichmüller curve is the golden eigenform locus, which contains the decagon locus. ∎

The strategy of the proof will be to show that it is always possible to find a translation surface in ℳ′\mathcal{M}^{\prime} where the periodic point coincides with a Weierstrass point. This will imply that ℳ\mathcal{M} is the golden eigenform locus.

Lemma 2.6.

The core curve of every cylinder in (X,ω)(X,\omega) contains exactly two Weierstrass points.

Proof.

Since (X,ω)(X,\omega) belongs to a hyperelliptic component, the core curve of every cylinder is fixed by the hyperelliptic involution, which is an orientation reversing isometry of the core curve. The result follows since every orientation reversing isometry of a circle has exactly two fixed points. ∎

Proposition 2.7.

Let (X,ω)(X,\omega) be the golden tetromino. Let (Xt,ωt)(X_{t},\omega_{t}) be the translation surface obtained by flowing along t​ρt\rho for tt some value in (−ϕ2,1)(-\phi^{2},1). Then (Xt,ωt)(X_{t},\omega_{t}) belongs to the decagon locus if and only if t=0t=0.

Proof.

The decagon locus has only two cusps, one which corresponds to a three-cylinder direction with ratio of moduli [1:1:2][1:1:2] and a second corresponding to a two-cylinder direction with identical moduli. Since the three horizontal cylinders persists for all tt in (−ϕ2,1)(-\phi^{2},1), if (Xt,ωt)(X_{t},\omega_{t}) lies in the decagon locus then their ratio of moduli must be [1:1:2][1:1:2]. At time tt the modulus of the topmost cylinder is 1−t1-t and the modulus of the bottommost is 2−tϕ2-\frac{t}{\phi}. Since 1−t<2−tϕ1-t<2-\frac{t}{\phi} for all t>−ϕ2t>-\phi^{2}, it follows that (Xt,ωt)(X_{t},\omega_{t}) belongs to the decagon locus only if 2​(1−t)=2−tϕ2(1-t)=2-\frac{t}{\phi}. The only solution to this equation is t=0t=0. ∎

Lemma 2.8.

The marked point does not lie on the boundary of a horizontal cylinder for its entire ρ\rho orbit.

Proof.

Suppose not to a contradiction. By Assumption 2.3, (X,ω)(X,\omega) has a vertical saddle connection ζ\zeta whose period tends to zero under forward ρ\rho-flow. Let (X′,ω′,p′)(X^{\prime},\omega^{\prime};p^{\prime}) be the marked translation surface in the boundary of ℳ′\mathcal{M}^{\prime} that forms when the period of ζ\zeta vanishes under the forward ρ\rho orbit of (X,ω,p)(X,\omega;p). By Proposition 2.4, p′p^{\prime} is a Weierstrass point. Since the Weierstrass points move continuously, there is a well-defined Weierstrass point qq on (X,ω)(X,\omega) so that pp and qq coincide on (X′,ω′)(X^{\prime},\omega^{\prime}).

Cylinders C2C_{2} and C3C_{3} persist on (X′,ω′)(X^{\prime},\omega^{\prime}). By Lemma 2.6, there are two Weierstrass points in their interiors on (X′,ω′)(X^{\prime},\omega^{\prime}). The other two Weierstrass points on (X′,ω′)(X^{\prime},\omega^{\prime}) occur at the unique zero of ω′\omega^{\prime} and at the midpoint of the saddle connection that connected C1C_{1} and C2C_{2} on (X,ω)(X,\omega).

We have assumed that the marked point lies on the boundary of a horizontal cylinder under forward ρ\rho flow. Therefore, it cannot coincide with a zero on (X′,ω′)(X^{\prime},\omega^{\prime}) since it would have to be a zero on (X,ω)(X,\omega). It follows that pp lies at the midpoint of one of the two horizontal saddle connections on (X,ω)(X,\omega) that connect C1C_{1} and C2C_{2} (see Figure 4).

Let qq be the Weierstrass point on (X,ω)(X,\omega) that merges with pp on (X′,ω′)(X^{\prime},\omega^{\prime}). Let γ\gamma be the vertical line that travels up from pp to qq. For any sufficiently small perturbation of (X,ω)(X,\omega) that keeps ζ\zeta vertical, Proposition 2.4 implies that using forward ρ\rho flow to shrink ζ\zeta causes pp and qq to coincide exactly when ζ\zeta vanishes. Since the period of γ\gamma vanishes exactly when the period of ζ\zeta vanishes, ℳ′\mathcal{M}^{\prime} locally satisfies the equation γ=ζ2\gamma=\frac{\zeta}{2}. Now, horizontally shear the surface (as in Figure 5) so that pp and a zero are on a vertical line contained in C1C_{1}.

Flow forward under ρ\rho until the height of C1C_{1} becomes zero. Call the new translation surface (Y,η)(Y,\eta). Since no saddle connection has vanished, (Y,η)(Y,\eta) does not belong to the boundary of ℳ\mathcal{M}. Moreover, the equation γ=ζ2\gamma=\frac{\zeta}{2} implies that pp and zz coincide on (Y,η)(Y,\eta). By Proposition 2.4, (Y,η)(Y,\eta) must belong to a Teichmüller curve and hence it belongs to the decagon locus and so ℳ\mathcal{M} is the golden eigenform locus.

When ℳ\mathcal{M} is the golden eigenform locus, Assumption 2.3 implies that (X,ω)(X,\omega) is a surface on the ρ\rho orbit of the golden tetromino. Since pp is fixed under ρ\rho flow at the midpoint of one of the two saddle connections that connect C1C_{1} and C2C_{2} it remains that point on the golden tetromino. However, this point is not a Weierstrass point on the golden tetromino and hence not a periodic point by Möller [Möl06]. This is a contradiction. ∎

In light of Lemma 2.8, we make the following assumption.

Assumption 2.9.

Suppose without loss of generality, possibly after flowing along ρ\rho for an arbitrarily small amount of time, that pp belongs to the interior of a horizontal cylinder on (X,ω)(X,\omega).

Lemma 2.10.

The marked point remains in the interior of a single cylinder for its entire ρ\rho orbit.

Proof.

Suppose it does not, i.e. there is a real number tt so that for all ss in [0,t][0,t], the three horizontal cylinders persist on s​ρ⋅(X,ω)s\rho\cdot(X,\omega) and so that at time tt the marked point reaches the boundary of one cylinder, say CC. The proof will proceed in three steps. First we will show that ℳ\mathcal{M} must be the golden eigenform locus. Second we will show that the marked point only reaches the boundary of a cylinder on the golden tetromino (X0,ω0)(X_{0},\omega_{0}). We show too that flowing backwards along ρ\rho from (X0,ω0)(X_{0},\omega_{0}) the marked point must be contained in the middle horizontal cylinder. Finally, we show that even this cannot occur.

Step 1: ℳ\mathcal{M} is the golden eigenform locus

Let zz be a zero on the boundary of the cylinder that pp reaches at time tt (see Figure 6).

Shear so that CC contains a vertical line joining pp and zz, as in Figure 7.

Flow along ρ\rho so that the marked point pp moves straight into zero at time ss. Since all three horizontal cylinders persist and the periodic point has been moved into a zero, ℳ\mathcal{M} must contain a Teichmüller curve by Proposition 2.4. Therefore, ℳ\mathcal{M} is the golden eigenform locus. Recall that we have assumed in this case that (X,ω)(X,\omega) is a surface given by applying ρ\rho for some amount of time to the golden tetromino. Assume specifically that (X,ω)=−ρ⋅(X0,ω0)(X,\omega)=-\rho\cdot(X_{0},\omega_{0}) where (X0,ω0)(X_{0},\omega_{0}) is the golden tetromino.

Step 2: pp belongs to the middle horizontal cylinder on (X,ω)(X,\omega)

By Proposition 2.7, the ρ\rho flow from the golden tetromino lies in the decagon locus only at time zero. Therefore, the previous argument implies that the only surface on the ρ\rho flow of the golden tetromino on which pp meets the boundary of a horizontal cylinder is on the golden tetromino itself. Suppose to a contradiction that this occurs.

Since the only periodic points on the golden tetromino are Weierstrass points, it follows that pp must collide with a zero on the golden tetromino. In particular, this implies that it lies on a vertical separatrix. Suppose to a contradiction that pp belongs to cylinder CC that is not the middle cylinder C2C_{2}. Let ξ\xi be the dashed saddle connection depicted in Figure 8

Shear so that the saddle connection ξ\xi is vertical and then flow backwards along ρ\rho to collapse ξ\xi - forming a boundary translation surface (Y,η)(Y,\eta). The boundary translation surface (Y,η)(Y,\eta) belongs to a eigenform locus in ℋ⁡(2)\mathcal{H}(2). By Proposition 2.4 the marked point pp must coincide with a Weierstrass point ww on (Y,η)(Y,\eta). By abuse of notation, we will let ww be the Weierstrass point on (X,ω)(X,\omega) that pp collides with under this degeneration.

We will argue that ww is contained in the interior of the cylinder CC that contains pp. This follows immediately from the observation that on (Y,η)(Y,\eta) the periodic point pp must lie exactly on the central horizontal curve in CC. If this did not happen, then under reverse ρ\rho flow starting at the golden tetromino, pp would travel from one boundary curve of CC to another. However, that would imply that pp at some point passed through a Weierstrass point. By Proposition 2.4 that can happen if and only if the underlying translation surface becomes a Veech surface, but by Proposition 2.7 that cannot happen.

Let γ\gamma be the straight line path from pp to ww that is contained in the cylinder CC and whose period goes to zero as the period of ξ\xi tends to zero. There is a constant cc so that γ=c​ξ\gamma=c\xi holds on all surfaces in a neighborhood of (X,ω,p)(X,\omega;p) in ℳ′\mathcal{M}^{\prime}. In particular, the slope of γ\gamma coincides with the slope of ξ\xi. However, passing to the golden tetromino under forward ρ\rho flow from (X,ω)(X,\omega) we have that γ\gamma has rational slope (since pp is contained in C1C_{1} or C3C_{3}) and ξ\xi has irrational slope. This contradicts the fact that γ\gamma are ξ\xi are parallel. Suppose therefore that pp lies in the middle horizontal cylinder on (X,ω)(X,\omega).

Step 3: pp cannot belong to the middle horizontal cylinder on (X,ω)(X,\omega)

Without loss of generality suppose that pp lies in the upper half of the middle horizontal cylinder and that pp intersects the top boundary of that cylinder under forward ρ\rho flow to the golden tetromino. Shear the surface so that there is a Weierstrass point ww in C1C_{1} that lies directly above pp. Call the resulting surface (Y,η)(Y,\eta) and let γ\gamma be the vertical line from pp to ww, see Figure 9.

Let (Yt,ηt)(Y_{t},\eta_{t}) be the surface that is the time tt flow along ρ\rho starting at the (Y,η)(Y,\eta). Recall that we chose (X,ω)(X,\omega) so that at time 11 under the forward ρ\rho flow it would become the golden tetromino. The computation in Proposition 2.7 shows that the only time tt in [0,2][0,2] for which two horizontal cylinders in (Yt,ηt)(Y_{t},\eta_{t}) have identical moduli is time 11. As mentioned in that proof, any three-cylinder direction in the decagon locus contains two cylinders of identical moduli. Therefore, (Yt,ηt)(Y_{t},\eta_{t}) belongs to the decagon locus only at time 11.

Notice that pp belongs to the interior of C1C_{1} and is moving upward for all time t>1t>1 (by moving upward we mean that the height of the point relative to the height of C1C_{1} is increasing). Since ww lies directly above pp and lies on the core curve of C1C_{1} we see that pp and ww must collide before C1C_{1} fully collapses. By Proposition 2.4 when pp and ww collide the underlying translation surface must belong to the decagon locus. However, we have already argued that (Yt,ηt)(Y_{t},\eta_{t}) does not belong to the decagon locus for t>1t>1, which is a contradiction.

∎

Recall our standing assumption (Assumption 2.3) that (X,ω)(X,\omega) is a surface with a vertical saddle connection ζ\zeta whose length tends to zero as we flow along ρ\rho.

Lemma 2.11.

The marked point is not contained in the topmost cylinder.

Proof.

Let (Y,η)(Y,\eta) be the translation surface on the boundary of ℳ\mathcal{M} that is formed when the period of ζ\zeta vanishes under forward ρ\rho flow. By Proposition 2.4 the periodic point pp must coincide with a Weierstrass point on (Y,η)(Y,\eta). In particular, this means that it must lie on a vertical separatrix contained in C1C_{1} joining pp to a Weierstrass point. Shear the surface to perform one complete Dehn twist in C1C_{1}. If there is still a vertical separatrix contained in C1C_{1} joining pp to a Weierstrass point then pp must itself be a Weierstrass point or a zero of ω\omega. Since pp is neither, it does not lie directly above or below a Weierstrass point after the shear is performed. Therefore, flowing under forward ρ\rho flow from the sheared surface collapses a vertical saddle connection contained in C1C_{1} and passes to a Teichmüller curve in the boundary of ℳ\mathcal{M}, but it does not cause the periodic point to coincide with a Weierstrass point on the boundary translation surface. This contradicts Proposition 2.4. ∎

The previous two lemmas are sufficient to classify the periodic points in the golden eigenform locus.

Proposition 2.12.

The only periodic points in the golden eigenform locus are the golden points.

Proof.

Let (X0,ω0)(X_{0},\omega_{0}) be the golden tetromino and let (Xt,ωt):=t​ρ⋅(X0,ω0)(X_{t},\omega_{t}):=t\rho\cdot(X_{0},\omega_{0}) for tt in (−ϕ2,1)(-\phi^{2},1). By Lemma 2.10, pp remains in the interior of a single horizontal cylinder for all tt. By Lemma 2.11 this cylinder is not the topmost cylinder. By Möller [Möl06], on (X0,ω0)(X_{0},\omega_{0}) the marked point coincides with a Weierstrass point in the interior of C2C_{2} or C3C_{3}. On (X1,ω1)(X_{1},\omega_{1}) the saddle connection ζ\zeta has vanished and so pp must coincide with a Weierstrass point or zero by Proposition 2.4. Therefore, on the golden tetromino, the periodic point pp is one of two Weierstrass points shown as black dots in Figure 10

Suppose first that the marked point pp coincides with w1w_{1} on the golden tetromino. Perturb slightly using ρ\rho so that the marked point now lies slightly above or below w1w_{1}. Shear the vertical cylinders so that one complete Dehn twist is performed about each vertical cylinder - this is possible since the vertical cylinders have identical moduli. The marked point now is contained in C1C_{1} on the ρ\rho-orbit of the golden tetromino, which contradicts Lemma 2.11.

Therefore, the marked point must coincide with w2w_{2} on the golden tetromino. Since the periodic point coincides with a zero zz on the boundary of C3C_{3} when t=1t=1, we see that if γ\gamma is the straight line between pp and zz, that ℳ′\mathcal{M}^{\prime} satisfies the equation γ=ϕ​ζ\gamma=\phi\zeta. By Kumar-Mukamel [KM16], this equation defines the golden points. ∎

Since we established Theorem 1 for the golden eigenform locus, we will make the following standing assumption for the remainder of the section:

Assumption 2.13.

ℳ\mathcal{M} is not the golden eigenform locus

Our goal will be to derive a contradiction from this assumption and Assumption 2.2.

Lemma 2.14.

The marked point remains in either the top or bottom half of a single horizontal cylinder.

Proof.

Suppose not to a contradiction and suppose without loss of generality that pp begins in the top half of a cylinder a crosses to the bottom half under forward ρ\rho flow. Shear the surface so that pp lies above a Weierstrass point. Flowing by ρ\rho now causes the marked point pp to collide with a Weierstrass point without degenerating the surface. By Proposition 2.4, ℳ\mathcal{M} contains a Teichmüller curve. However, the golden eigenform locus is the only such eigenform locus and ℳ\mathcal{M} is not that locus by Assumption 2.13. ∎

Lemma 2.15.

The marked point is not contained in the middle horizontal cylinder.

Proof.

Suppose not to a contradiction. Assume without loss of generality (possibly using the hyperelliptic involution) that pp belongs to the top half of the middle cylinder. Let BB be the top boundary of the cylinder.

Case 1: pp moves towards BB under forward ρ\rho flow

By assumption, the distance between pp and BB decreases under forward ρ\rho flow (and so it increases under backwards ρ\rho flow). Under backwards ρ\rho flow the height of the middle cylinder tends to zero. Therefore, shear the surface so that pp lies directly above a Weierstrass point contained in the middle cylinder and flow backwards along ρ\rho. Since the distance from the Weierstrass point and BB tends to zero and the distance between pp and BB increases, pp must collide with a Weierstrass point before the surface degenerates. By Proposition 2.4, ℳ\mathcal{M} contains a Teichmüller curve and this contradicts Assumption 2.13.

Case 2: pp moves towards the core curve under forward ρ\rho flow

Shear the middle horizontal cylinder so that it contains a vertical saddle connection ξ\xi with the property that sending the period of ξ\xi to zero under reverse ρ\rho flow passes to a boundary translation surface in ℋ⁡(2)\mathcal{H}(2), see Figure 11. By Proposition 2.4, pp collides with a Weierstrass point on the boundary and therefore pp lies directly above a Weierstrass point contained in the middle horizontal cylinder.

Shear the surface so as to perform one complete Dehn twist in the middle horizontal cylinder. As before it is still necessarily the case that pp lies directly above a Weierstrass point contained in the middle horizontal cylinder. Since pp belongs to the interior of the middle horizontal cylinder, pp lies directly above a Weierstrass point both before and after the shear if and only if pp is a Weierstrass point, which is a contradiction.

∎

Proof of Theorem 1:

By Lemmas 2.11 and 2.15 we may suppose that pp is contained in the interior of the bottom horizontal cylinder. By Lemma 2.14 we suppose without loss of generality that pp is contained in the top half of the bottom horizontal cylinder for the entire ρ\rho flow. Let BB be the top boundary of the bottom horizontal cylinder. Let hih_{i} denote the height of CiC_{i} and let ℓi\ell_{i} be the length of its core curve. Suppose without loss of generality, after shearing, that the middle horizontal cylinder begins in the configuration shown in Figure 12.

Case 1: pp moves towards BB under forward ρ\rho flow

Suppose first that ℓ1<ℓ3\ell_{1}<\ell_{3}. After shearing by (1ℓ1h201)\begin{pmatrix}1&\frac{\ell_{1}}{h_{2}}\\ 0&1\end{pmatrix} we have the configuration shown in Figure 13.

Similarly shearing by (1ℓ3h201)\begin{pmatrix}1&\frac{\ell_{3}}{h_{2}}\\ 0&1\end{pmatrix} we have the configuration shown in Figure 14.

In these two sheared configurations there is exactly one vertical saddle connection contained in the middle horizontal cylinder and so collapsing it under backwards ρ\rho flow passes to a Veech surface in ℋ⁡(2)\mathcal{H}(2) on the boundary of ℳ\mathcal{M}. By Proposition 2.4, on this boundary translation surface the periodic point coincides with a Weierstrass point. Therefore, in these two sheared configurations, pp lies directly above a Weierstrass point contained in C3C_{3}.

Let’s begin in the first sheared configuration (Figure 13). The marked point pp lies directly above a Weierstrass point ww. Let w′w^{\prime} be the other Weierstrass point contained in the bottom horizontal cylinder. As we continue to shear the surface if at some point pp lies above w′w^{\prime}, then C2C_{2} must contain a vertical saddle connection (if not we can apply reverse ρ\rho flow to cause the periodic point to coincide with a Weierstrass point while remaining in ℳ\mathcal{M}; this contradicts Assumption 2.13). Conversely, if C2C_{2} contains exactly one vertical saddle connection, then pp must lie above a Weierstrass point since collapsing C2C_{2} using reverse ρ\rho flow passes to a Veech surface in ℋ⁡(2)\mathcal{H}(2). These two observations imply that as we shear from the first sheared configuration to the second the periodic point goes from lying directly above ww to lying directly above w′w^{\prime} without lying over a Weierstrass point at any other point along the way. In other words, the matrix (1ℓ3−ℓ1h201)\begin{pmatrix}1&\frac{\ell_{3}-\ell_{1}}{h_{2}}\\ 0&1\end{pmatrix} moves the marked point a horizontal distance of ℓ32\frac{\ell_{3}}{2} to the right of ww. This implies that the marked point lies at height h2​ℓ32​(ℓ3−ℓ1)\frac{h_{2}\ell_{3}}{2\left(\ell_{3}-\ell_{1}\right)} above ww.

However, beginning in the first sheared configuration and doing a complete Dehn twist also moves the periodic point by an integer multiple of ℓ32\frac{\ell_{3}}{2} horizontally with respect to ww, which implies that pp lies at height n​h2​ℓ32​(ℓ3+ℓ1)\frac{nh_{2}\ell_{3}}{2\left(\ell_{3}+\ell_{1}\right)} above ww, where nn is an integer. These two equations for the height of pp above ww imply that ℓ3−ℓ1ℓ3+ℓ1\frac{\ell_{3}-\ell_{1}}{\ell_{3}+\ell_{1}} is a rational number, which occurs if and only if ℓ1ℓ3\frac{\ell_{1}}{\ell_{3}} is rational. However, this cannot be since this would imply that the original surface is arithmetic, contradicting Assumption 2.1. The case of ℓ3<ℓ1\ell_{3}<\ell_{1} is identical except the expression ℓ3−ℓ1\ell_{3}-\ell_{1} is replaced with ℓ1−ℓ3\ell_{1}-\ell_{3}. The case of ℓ1=ℓ3\ell_{1}=\ell_{3} cannot occur since this again would force the translation surface to be a torus cover.

Case 2: pp moves towards the core curve under forward ρ\rho flow

When ζ\zeta vanishes under forward ρ\rho flow, the translation surface becomes a nonarithmetic eigenform in ℋ⁡(2)\mathcal{H}(2). By Proposition 2.4, when this happens, the marked point must coincide with a Weierstrass point in the interior of C3C_{3}.

Now shear (X,ω)(X,\omega) so that C1C_{1} contains no vertical saddle connection. Flow forward using ρ\rho until just after the height of C1C_{1} has become zero. Call the resulting translation surface (Y,η)(Y,\eta). It is shown in Figure 15. Opposite sides are identified unless otherwise specified. Solid dots in the bottom cylinder are Weierstrass points.

Relabel the horizontal cylinders in (Y,η)(Y,\eta) as in Figure 15 and, for i∈{1,2,3}i\in\{1,2,3\}, let γi′\gamma_{i}^{\prime} denote the core curve of Ci′C_{i}^{\prime} oriented from left to right. Notice that continuing to flow along ρ\rho is the same as flowing along ρ′:=−i⁡(γ1′−γ2′+γ3′)\rho^{\prime}:=-i\left(\gamma_{1}^{\prime}-\gamma_{2}^{\prime}+\gamma_{3}^{\prime}\right). After shearing so that the shorter cylinder of {C1′,C3′}\{C_{1}^{\prime},C_{3}^{\prime}\} contains a vertical saddle connection we notice that (Y,η)(Y,\eta) satisfies Assumptions 2.2, 2.3. and 2.9. If C3′C_{3}^{\prime} is shorter than C1′C_{1}^{\prime} then we contradict Lemma 2.11. Otherwise, pp is contained in the bottom half of C3′C_{3}^{\prime} and moves towards the bottom boundary as the height of C1′C_{1}^{\prime} decreases. This is Case 1 of this proof; hence we have a contradiction as desired.

∎

3. Proof of Theorem 4 - The Finite Blocking Problem in Genus Two

The finite blocking problem asks whether given two points pp and qq on a translation surface (X,ω)(X,\omega) there is a finite collection of points BB on (X,ω)(X,\omega) so that all straight line paths between pp and qq contain a point in BB? In this section we will solve the finite blocking problem for genus two translation surfaces by proving Theorem 4.

Since this theorem was established in Apisa [Apia] for genus two translation surfaces in ℋ⁡(2)\mathcal{H}(2) and ℋ⁡(1,1)\mathcal{H}(1,1) whose GL2⁡(ℝ)\GL_{2}(\mathbb{R}) orbit is dense, it suffices to consider genus two translation surfaces whose orbit closures are neither the entire stratum nor a locus of torus covers. These translation surfaces were classified by McMullen in  [McM06] and [McM07]; in particular, the orbit closures of these translation surfaces are exactly the collection of eigenforms for real multiplication by an order in a quadratic field. These loci are classified by the (non-square) discriminant DD of the order and have either one or two connected components depending on whether DD is not or is congruent to 11 mod 88 respectively.

We will now outline our approach to the finite blocking problem. By Möller [Möl06, Theorem 2.6], if (X,ω)(X,\omega) is not a torus cover, then there is a unique map πXmin:(X,ω)→(Xmin,ωmin)\pi_{X_{\operatorname{min}}}:(X,\omega)\to(X_{\operatorname{min}},\omega_{\operatorname{min}}) to a translation surface of minimal genus, and any map from (X,ω)(X,\omega) to a translation surface is a factor of this map. In Apisa-Wright [AW17, Lemma 3.3], it was shown that similarly, when (X,ω)(X,\omega) is not a torus cover there is a quadratic differential (Qmin,qmin)(Q_{\operatorname{min}},q_{\operatorname{min}}) with a degree 1 or 2 map (Xmin,ωmin)→(Qmin,qmin)(X_{\operatorname{min}},\omega_{\operatorname{min}})\to(Q_{\operatorname{min}},q_{\operatorname{min}}) such that any map from (X,ω)(X,\omega) to a quadratic differential is a factor of the composite map πQmin:(X,ω)→(Qmin,qmin)\pi_{Q_{\operatorname{min}}}:(X,\omega)\to(Q_{\operatorname{min}},q_{\operatorname{min}}). By Apisa-Wright [AW17, Theorems 3.5 and 3.15],

Theorem 3.1 (Apisa-Wright [AW17]).

If (X,ω)(X,\omega) is not a torus cover then

  1. (1)

    If pp is a periodic point or zero, it can only be finitely blocked from other periodic points or zeros and a blocking set is contained in the collection of periodic points.

  2. (2)

    If pp is not a periodic point, then it is only finitely blocked from other points in B1:=πQmin−1​(πQmin​(p))B_{1}:=\pi_{Q_{\operatorname{min}}}^{-1}\left(\pi_{Q_{\operatorname{min}}}(p)\right) and a blocking set is contained in the collection of periodic points along with the points in B1B_{1}

Since we are concerned with primitive translation surfaces (X,ω)(X,\omega), which is equivalent to not being a torus cover in genus two, we have that (Xmin,ωmin)=(X,ω)(X_{\operatorname{min}},\omega_{\operatorname{min}})=(X,\omega). Therefore, (Qmin,qmin)(Q_{\operatorname{min}},q_{\operatorname{min}}) is the quotient of (X,ω)(X,\omega) be the hyperelliptic involution. This shows the following:

Proposition 3.2.

If (X,ω)(X,\omega) is a genus two translation surface that belongs to an eigenform locus then two points are finitely blocked only if they are exchanged by the hyperelliptic involution or they are both periodic points or zeros (in which case the blocking set is the collection of periodic points).

Remark 3.3.

It is well-known that two points exchanged by the hyperelliptic involution are finitely blocked with a blocking set contained in the set of Weierstrass points (see for instance [AW17, Lemma 3.1]). Similarly, any Weierstrass point is blocked from itself by the other Weierstrass points. This reduces the proof of Theorem 4 to showing that no other pairs of periodic points are finitely blocked by the set of periodic points.

Lemma 3.4.

Suppose that ℳ\mathcal{M} is an orbit closure that is neither a locus of torus covers nor the golden eigenform locus and that contains a translation surface (X,ω)(X,\omega) that may be represented as a convex octagon or decagon with opposite sides identified. Then Theorem 4 holds for ℳ\mathcal{M}.

Proof.

Since Theorem 4 holds for ℳ\mathcal{M} a genus two stratum, suppose that ℳ\mathcal{M} is a nonarithmetic eigenform locus different from the golden eigenform locus. On (X,ω)(X,\omega), the Weierstrass points that are not singularities occur at midpoints of the edges of the nn-gon and at the midpoint of the face of the nn-gon. By Theorem 1 the only periodic points are Weierstrass points and hence by Remark 3.3 it suffices to show that the only pairs of periodic points and zeros that are finitely blocked by the collection of Weierstrass points are nonsingular Weierstrass points from themselves. The description of (X,ω)(X,\omega) as a convex polygon with opposite sides identified and the explicit description of the nonsingular Weierstrass points makes this immediate. ∎

Corollary 3.5.

Theorem 4 holds in ℋ⁡(1,1)\mathcal{H}(1,1).

Proof.

By Lelièvre and Weiss [LW15, Theorem 2], every nonarithmetic eigenform locus (and trivially the decagon locus) contains a translation surface that may be represented as a convex decagon with opposite sides identified. By Lemma 3.4, Theorem 4 holds for all surfaces in ℋ⁡(1,1)\mathcal{H}(1,1) except possibly those in the golden eigenform locus.

The golden point on the golden eigenform locus is not finitely blocked from itself because if it were then the blocking set could be taken to be the collection of periodic points in the golden eigenform locus, but we see in the left subfigure of Figure 16 that these points do not block the horizontal line from the golden point to itself.

To form the right subfigure, begin with the golden tetromino (the lefthand figure with t=0t=0) and horizontally shear so that the vertical cylinders become the dotted diagonal cylinders. Applying ρ\rho - the rel flow from the previous section - to the regular decagon we arrive at the righthand subfigure, where the golden points are on the vertical line passing through the midpoint of the decagon.

Since any blocking set is contained in the set of periodic points we see that point 55 is not blocked from any periodic point (consider the left half of the decagon) and similarly point 66 is not blocked from any periodic point. Finally, consider the part of the decagon that lies on or above the horizontal line through the upper golden point. This subsurface is convex and all periodic points excluding points 55, 66, and the lower golden point lie on the boundary. Therefore, none of these point are finitely blocked from any other. ∎

Proof of Theorem 4:

It remains to establish the claim in nonarithmetic eigenform loci in ℋ⁡(2)\mathcal{H}(2). By Möller [Möl06], the only periodic points in these loci are Weierstrass points. By Lelièvre and Weiss [LW15, Theorem 1], each nonarithmetic eigenform locus contains a generic translation surface that has a representation as a (not necessarily strictly) convex polygon with opposite sides identified except when D=5,12,17,21D=5,12,17,21, 32,410,45,7732,41_{0},45,77 where the subscript denotes the spin component (to be explained shortly). By Lemma 3.4, this establishes the theorem outside of these eight cases.

By McMullen [McM05, Theorem 3.3] each of these eigenform loci contains the surface in Figure 17 where bb, cc, ee are any integers (with bb and cc strictly positive and gcd⁡(b,c,e)=1\mathrm{gcd}(b,c,e)=1) such that the following hold:

  1. (1)

    λ=e+D2\displaystyle{\lambda=\frac{e+\sqrt{D}}{2}}

  2. (2)

    D=e2+4​b​cD=e^{2}+4bc

  3. (3)

    c+e<bc+e<b

  4. (4)

    If D=E​f2D=Ef^{2}, then the spin invariant is e−f2+(c+1)​b​ mod ​2\displaystyle{\frac{e-f}{2}+(c+1)b\text{ mod }2}.

The moduli of the two horizontal cylinders are 11 and cb\frac{c}{b}. The horizontal direction corresponds to a parabolic element of the Veech group. The parabolic element is just a product of Dehn twists about the core curves of the horizontal cylinders. If cb=c′b′\frac{c}{b}=\frac{c^{\prime}}{b^{\prime}} where c′c^{\prime} and b′b^{\prime} are coprime, then the Dehn twist is a complete c′c^{\prime}-twist about the top cylinder and a complete b′b^{\prime} twist about the lower cylinder. The element of the Veech group is (1b′01)\begin{pmatrix}1&b^{\prime}\\ 0&1\end{pmatrix}. Letting this Dehn multi twist act on the Weierstrass points, (and hence thinking about it as an element of a Sym⁡(5)\mathrm{Sym}(5)) we see that the action is (12)c′​(45)b′(12)^{c^{\prime}}(45)^{b^{\prime}}.

Similarly, in the vertical direction the modulus of the leftmost cylinder is λλ+c\frac{\lambda}{\lambda+c} and the modulus of the rightmost cylinder is b−λc\frac{b-\lambda}{c}. Denote these two cylinders by VℓV_{\ell} and VrV_{r} where the subscript denotes right and left.

Mod⁡(Vr)Mod⁡(Vℓ)=(b−λ)​(λ+c)c​λ\frac{\mathrm{Mod}(V_{r})}{\mathrm{Mod}(V_{\ell})}=\frac{(b-\lambda)(\lambda+c)}{c\lambda}

Recall that λ2=e​λ+b​c\lambda^{2}=e\lambda+bc, so

Mod⁡(Vr)Mod⁡(Vℓ)=b−c−ec\frac{\mathrm{Mod}(V_{r})}{\mathrm{Mod}(V_{\ell})}=\frac{b-c-e}{c}

Express this ratio in lowest terms as b′′c′′\frac{b^{\prime\prime}}{c^{\prime\prime}}. The corresponding Dehn multi twist is a complete b′′b^{\prime\prime} twist in the rightmost cylinder and a complete c′′c^{\prime\prime} twist in the leftmost. Letting this Dehn multi twist act on the Weierstrass points, (and hence thinking about it as an element of a Sym⁡(5)\mathrm{Sym}(5)) we see that the action is (23)c′′​(14)b′′(23)^{c^{\prime\prime}}(14)^{b^{\prime\prime}}.

Lemma 3.6.

If c′c^{\prime} and b′b^{\prime} or c′′c^{\prime\prime} and b′′b^{\prime\prime} are both odd, then no two distinct Weierstrass points are blocked from each other on (X,ω)(X,\omega).

Proof.

First, we see that the Weierstrass point marked 11 is not finitely blocked from any of the other Weierstrass points. If c′,c′′,b′,c^{\prime},c^{\prime\prime},b^{\prime}, and b′′b^{\prime\prime} are all odd, then the Dehn twists in the Veech group that we identified act on the Weierstrass point by the group generated by (23)​(14)(23)(14) and (12)​(45)(12)(45). Since {4,5}\{4,5\} illuminate each other we are done. In the second case, {1,2,4,5}\{1,2,4,5\} illuminate all other distinct Weierstrass points so we are done.

The case where c′′c^{\prime\prime} and b′′b^{\prime\prime} are both odd and either c′c^{\prime} or b′b^{\prime} is even is completely analogous. ∎

4. Proof of Theorem 5 - Hyperelliptic Curves and Holomorphic dd-differentials

In this section we will determine exactly which holomorphic dd-differentials unfold to hyperelliptic Riemann surfaces. We want our discussion to apply to billiards and so we use the approach of Mirzakhani-Wright [MW16, Section 6]. Given an nn-gon with connected boundary and with angles, specified in clockwise order, θ=(a1b1,…,anbn)⋅π\theta=\left(\frac{a_{1}}{b_{1}},\ldots,\frac{a_{n}}{b_{n}}\right)\cdot\pi where aia_{i} and bib_{i} are coprime pairs of integers for all ii, let ℳ⁡(θ)\mathcal{M}(\theta) be the smallest affine invariant submanifold containing all unfoldings of rational polygons with angles (ordered clockwise) θ\theta. Let dd to be the least common multiple of {bi}i=1n\{b_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}.

Lemma 4.1.

If θ\theta and θ′\theta^{\prime} are permutations of each other, then ℳ⁡(θ)\mathcal{M}(\theta) and ℳ⁡(θ′)\mathcal{M}(\theta^{\prime}) coincide.

Proof.

An unfolding is completely specified by its pillowcase double, which is a dd-differential on the Riemann sphere with all zeros on the real line. Suppose that PP belongs to a stratum 𝒬\mathcal{Q} of dd-differentials and let 𝒰⁡(θ)\mathcal{U}(\theta) be the collection of all such pillowcase doubles. Given the pillowcase double PP, all zeros may be moved freely on the real line by altering the lengths of the sides of BB. This shows that 𝒰⁡(θ)\mathcal{U}(\theta) is Zariski dense in 𝒬\mathcal{Q}. In particular, the Zariski closure of 𝒰⁡(θ)\mathcal{U}(\theta) contains 𝒰⁡(θ′)\mathcal{U}(\theta^{\prime}) since all strata of dd-differentials on the sphere are connected.

Let π:𝒬⟶ℋ\pi:\mathcal{Q}\longrightarrow\mathcal{H} be the map that associates to a dd-differential its canonical unfolding as an abelian differential. This map is holomorphic. By Filip [Fil16], ℳ⁡(θ)\mathcal{M}(\theta), which is the orbit closure of π⁡(𝒰⁡(θ))\pi\left(\mathcal{U}(\theta)\right), is a variety. In particular, ℳ⁡(θ)\mathcal{M}(\theta) contains the image of the Zariski closure of 𝒰⁡(θ)\mathcal{U}(\theta) under π\pi. Therefore, ℳ⁡(θ)\mathcal{M}(\theta) contains ℳ⁡(θ′)\mathcal{M}(\theta^{\prime}). By symmetry these two orbit closures coincide. ∎

In light of the lemma, we will relax our assumption that θ\theta be specified up to cyclic order and instead insist that it is specified as a set. By Lemma 4.1, the loci ℳ⁡(θ)\mathcal{M}(\theta) are precisely the smallest affine invariant submanifolds containing the unfoldings of all dd-differentials with the same singularity type as the pillowcase double of a polygon with angles θ\theta.

Given a dd-differential on the sphere, it canonically unfolds to a flat surface that is invariant under a ℤ/d​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/d\mathbb{Z} action, see [BCG+16, Section 2]. The quotient of the flat surface by the cyclic group is exactly the original dd-differential. If the dd-differential has singularities (a1​πb1,…,an​πbn)​2​π\left(\frac{a_{1}\pi}{b_{1}},\ldots,\frac{a_{n}\pi}{b_{n}}\right)2\pi where d=lcm⁡(b1,…,bn)d=\mathrm{lcm}\left(b_{1},\ldots,b_{n}\right) then a singularity of cone angle aibi⋅2​π\frac{a_{i}}{b_{i}}\cdot 2\pi has dbi\frac{d}{b_{i}} preimages each bib_{i}-ramified.

Lemma 4.2.

Suppose that PP is a dd-differential on the sphere with cone-angles (a1b1,…,anbn)⋅2​π\left(\frac{a_{1}}{b_{1}},\ldots,\frac{a_{n}}{b_{n}}\right)\cdot 2\pi. The deck group of the canonical covering contains a hyperelliptic involution if and only if d:=lcm⁡(b1,…,bn)=2​kd:=\mathrm{lcm}\left(b_{1},\ldots,b_{n}\right)=2k for some integer kk and (up to permutation) the cone angles are:

(a1d,a2d,a32,…,an2)​2​π\left(\frac{a_{1}}{d},\frac{a_{2}}{d},\frac{a_{3}}{2},\ldots,\frac{a_{n}}{2}\right)2\pi

where a3,…,ana_{3},\ldots,a_{n} are odd, a1a_{1} and a2a_{2} are positive integers coprime to kk, and k⁡(n−2)+m=2​g+2k(n-2)+m=2g+2 where mm is the number of odd integers in {a1,a2}\{a_{1},a_{2}\} and gg the genus of the canonical cover.

Proof.

Suppose first that the deck group contains the hyperelliptic involution. The deck group is then a cyclic group of order d=2​kd=2k, since it contains an involution. Quotienting by the hyperelliptic involution gives a quadratic differential (Q,q)(Q,q) on the sphere with 2​g+22g+2 singularities of cone angle an odd multiple of π\pi. The deck group descends to a cyclic group of order kk of automorphisms that preserve (Q,q)(Q,q). Up to Möbius transformations, the map from (Q,q)(Q,q) to PP must be given by f⁡(z)=zkf(z)=z^{k}. Since PP pulls back to a quadratic differential under f⁡(z)=zkf(z)=z^{k} it follows that the singularities at 00 and ∞\infty have the form ai2​k⋅2​π\frac{a_{i}}{2k}\cdot 2\pi for some integer aia_{i} (i=1,2i=1,2) and that all other singularities have the form ai2⋅2​π\frac{a_{i}}{2}\cdot 2\pi for some integer aia_{i} (i>3i>3). Pulling back the dd-differential to a quadratic differential on the sphere gives k⁡(n−2)+mk(n-2)+m points with odd cone angle, which must be Weierstrass points under the double cover. This implies that k⁡(n−2)+m=2​g+2k(n-2)+m=2g+2.

For the reverse direction, the canonical cover by a quadratic differential must be the cyclic cover which is kk ramified over a1d\frac{a_{1}}{d} and a2d\frac{a_{2}}{d}. The canonical cover of this quadratic differential is a hyperelliptic abelian differential (X,ω)(X,\omega) and the map from (X,ω)(X,\omega) to PP has the same branching as the canonical cover of PP; therefore this cover must be the canonical one. ∎

Lemma 4.4.

Let PP be a dd-differential on the sphere. The canonical cover contains a hyperelliptic involution that is not part of the deck group if and only if BB is not the double of a rectangle or the 45−45−9045-45-90 triangle and the singularities are either (a1d,a1d,a2d,a2d)​2​π\left(\frac{a_{1}}{d},\frac{a_{1}}{d},\frac{a_{2}}{d},\frac{a_{2}}{d}\right)2\pi or (a1d,a1d,a2d)​2​π\left(\frac{a_{1}}{d},\frac{a_{1}}{d},\frac{a_{2}}{d}\right)2\pi where aia_{i} are positive integers so that a1a_{1} is coprime to dd.

and the singularities of P′P^{\prime} are

where the first two singularities lie at {0,∞}\{0,\infty\} and π\pi is branched over the last two. The first two singularities in P′P^{\prime} have at most two preimages on (X,ω)(X,\omega) and hence a1a_{1} and b1b_{1} are coprime to dd.

For the reverse direction, both of the dd-differentials described have an involution so that the quotient map π:P⟶P′\pi:P\longrightarrow P^{\prime} sends PP to a 2​d2d-differential P′P^{\prime} with singularities θ′=(a1d,a2d,12,12)​2​π\theta^{\prime}=\left(\frac{a_{1}}{d},\frac{a_{2}}{d},\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}\right)2\pi or θ′=(a1d,a22​d,12)\theta^{\prime}=\left(\frac{a_{1}}{d},\frac{a_{2}}{2d},\frac{1}{2}\right) where a1a_{1} is a positive integer coprime to dd.
