5. Proof of Theorem 6 - Billiard Tables Unfolding to Genus Two Surfaces

We will now solve the finite blocking problem for rational polygons that unfold to genus two translation surfaces.

Definition 5.1.

A rational polygon that unfolds to a hyperelliptic Riemann surface will be called “special” if the group of deck transformations does not include the hyperelliptic involution

The list of special rational polygons is given in Lemma 4.4.

Proposition 5.2.

Suppose that BB is a polygon with connected boundary with rational angles θ=(a1b1,…,anbn)⋅π\theta=\left(\frac{a_{1}}{b_{1}},\ldots,\frac{a_{n}}{b_{n}}\right)\cdot\pi that unfolds to a hyperelliptic Riemann surface. Suppose that any point pp on the unfolding of BB is finitely blocked from no points if it is a zero and only finitely blocked from its image under the hyperelliptic involution otherwise. Define d:=lcm⁡(b1,…,bn)d:=\mathrm{lcm}(b_{1},\ldots,b_{n}). The following is a complete list of the pairs of finitely blocked points on BB:

  1. (1)

    If BB is not special any vertex of angle πd\frac{\pi}{d} is finitely blocked from itself.

  2. (2)

    If BB is special any two distinct vertices of angle πd\frac{\pi}{d} are finitely blocked from each other.

  3. (3)

    If BB is an isosceles triangle and the non-repeated angle has the form πd\frac{\pi}{d}, then this vertex is finitely blocked from itself.

Proof.

Suppose first that pp and qq are two distinct points on BB that are finitely blocked from each other. Let p~\widetilde{p} be a preimage of pp on the unfolding of BB. Since p~\widetilde{p} is finitely blocked from at most one other point it follows that there is exactly one preimage of qq on the unfolding of BB. By symmetry of hypotheses, there must also be exactly one preimage of pp as well. A point on BB has exactly one preimage on the unfolding if and only if it corresponds to a vertex of angle πd\frac{\pi}{d}. There are two vertices of cone angle πd\frac{\pi}{d} only if d=2d=2, d=4d=4, or BB is special. If BB is not special then the preimage of pp is a Weierstrass point and hence only finitely blocked from itself, a contradiction since it is also blocked from the preimage of qq. Therefore, BB is special and the two vertices of angle πd\frac{\pi}{d} unfold to two points exchanged by the hyperelliptic involution, which are hence finitely blocked from each other.

Suppose now that pp is a point on BB that is finitely blocked from itself. By hypothesis, p~\widetilde{p} must contain one non-singular Weierstrass point and hence pp is a vertex of angle πd\frac{\pi}{d}. Such a point becomes a nonsingular Weierstrass point when BB is not special or if BB is an isosceles triangle and the vertex is the one corresponding to the non-repeated angle. ∎

Proof of Theorem 6.

The list of rational polygons with connected boundary that unfold to a genus two translation surface in Figure 1 is complete by Corollaries 4.3 and 4.6.

We begin with the claim about when an unfolding is a torus cover. By Apisa-Wright [AW17, Theorem 1.1] (see also Proposition 3.10 in Apisa-Wright [AW17]), if a rational polygon unfolds to a torus cover it in fact unfolds to a square tiled surface. This implies that the ℚ\mathbb{Q}-linear span of the relative periods is a two-dimensional ℚ\mathbb{Q}-vector space. Therefore, the ratio of lengths x1x2\frac{x_{1}}{x_{2}} and y1y2\frac{y_{1}}{y_{2}} must be rational. For the converse, we observe that when these ratios are rational we may scale the figure so that the relative periods of the unfolding lie in either the Gaussian or Eisenstein integers, which implies that the unfolding is a square-tiled surface.

The claim about finite blocking for polygons that unfold to genus two translation surfaces follows from Proposition 5.2 and Theorem 4 (which certifies that the hypotheses in the statement of the proposition are satisfied).

The computation of ℳ⁡(θ)\mathcal{M}(\theta) in Figure 1 follows in all cases from either the definition of the given locus or from the “trivial rank bound” in Mirzakhani-Wright [MW16, Lemma 7.1], which states that if there is some entry of θ\theta that is not an integer multiple of π2\frac{\pi}{2}, then ℳ⁡(θ)\mathcal{M}(\theta) has rank at least |θ|−2|\theta|-2 where |θ||\theta| is the length of θ\theta. In genus two strata of translation surfaces the only affine invariant submanifold that has rank two is the entire stratum itself. ∎

6. Similar Cylinders

It remains to show that there is at most one non-arithmetic rank two affine invariant submanifold in ℋ⁡(6)\mathcal{H}(6). Before proving that statement, we first prove an independently interesting cylinder lemma. The idea for the lemma arose from conversations with Alex Wright.

We begin by summarizing some facts about cylinder deformations. Fix an affine invariant submanifold ℳ\mathcal{M}. By Avila-Eskin-Möller [AEM], the projection of the tangent space of ℳ\mathcal{M} to absolute cohomology is complex symplectic. The rank of ℳ\mathcal{M} is defined to be half the complex dimension of this projection. The affine invariant submanifold is said to have dd dimensions of rel, if d=dimℂℳ−2​rd=\dim_{\mathbb{C}}\mathcal{M}-2r where rr is the rank of ℳ\mathcal{M}.

On a translation surface in ℳ\mathcal{M}, two cylinders are said to be equivalent if on all nearby translation surfaces in ℳ\mathcal{M} their core curves are parallel. A maximal set of equivalent cylinders is called an equivalence class of cylinders.

Definition 6.1.

Fix an equivalence class of cylinders with core curves {γi}i=1n\{\gamma_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n} - all of whose periods differ up to scaling by a positive real number - and heights {hi}i=1n\{h_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}. The standard shear, which is defined up to scaling by a nonzero complex scalar, refers to the cohomology class ∑i=1nhi​γi∗\sum_{i=1}^{n}h_{i}\gamma_{i}^{*} where γi∗\gamma_{i}^{*} is the cohomology class corresponding to intersections with γi\gamma_{i} for i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n.

By Wright [Wri15, Theorem 1.1], the standard shear always belongs to the tangent space of ℳ\mathcal{M}. By Wright [Wri15, Theorem 1.10], if ℳ\mathcal{M} is a rank rr affine invariant submanifold then there is always a translation surface (X,ω)(X,\omega) in ℳ\mathcal{M} that is horizontally periodic, with rr horizontal equivalence classes, and so that the standard shears of the horizontal equivalence classes project to a Lagrangian subspace in the projection of T(X,ω)​ℳT_{(X,\omega)}\mathcal{M} to absolute cohomology. These properties are actually implied by a stronger condition, i.e. that the “twist space and cylinder preserving space of (X,ω)(X,\omega) coincide”, see Wright [Wri15] for a definition.

Definition 6.2.

Two cylinders C1C_{1} and C2C_{2} on a translation surface are similar if the two cylinders, with boundaries marked at cone points, are rescaled versions of each other, i.e. if there is some positive real number λ\lambda so that C1=(λ00λ)​C2C_{1}=\begin{pmatrix}\lambda&0\\ 0&\lambda\end{pmatrix}C_{2}.

The aim of this section is to show that if two simple cylinders form an equivalence class on a translation surface whose orbit closure has no rel, then the two cylinders are similar.

Assumption 6.3.

Let ℳ\mathcal{M} be an affine invariant submanifold with no rel and that has rank r>1r>1.

Lemma 6.4.

Let 𝒞\mathcal{C} be an ℳ\mathcal{M}-equivalence class of cylinders on a translation surface (X,ω)∈ℳ(X,\omega)\in\mathcal{M}. Let UU be a connected neighborhood of (X,ω)(X,\omega) in ℳ\mathcal{M} on which the cylinders in 𝒞\mathcal{C} persist (i.e. their heights never reach zero). Then for each surface in UU, 𝒞\mathcal{C} remains an ℳ\mathcal{M}-equivalence class of cylinders.

Proof.

Suppose to a contradiction that there is a point (Y,η)(Y,\eta) in UU, in which 𝒞\mathcal{C} fails to be an equivalence class, i.e. there is a superset 𝒞′\mathcal{C}^{\prime} of 𝒞\mathcal{C} that is an equivalence class. By Mirzakhani-Wright [MW17, Corollary 1.5], the ratio of moduli of two ℳ\mathcal{M}-equivalent cylinders is locally constant in ℳ\mathcal{M}. Let γ\gamma be a path in UU from (Y,η)(Y,\eta) to (X,ω)(X,\omega). Since the ratio of moduli of cylinders in 𝒞′\mathcal{C}^{\prime} is constant, if one cylinder fails to persist then all of them must. Some cylinders must fail to persist along this path since 𝒞\mathcal{C} is an equivalence class at (X,ω)(X,\omega). However, by assumption the cylinders in 𝒞\mathcal{C} persist along the path and so we have a contradiction. ∎

Suppose that (X,ω)(X,\omega) is a translation surface in ℳ\mathcal{M} that is horizontally periodic and that has cylinder preserving space and twist space coinciding. By Avila-Eskin-Möller [AEM], the projection of the tangent space of ℳ\mathcal{M} to absolute cohomology is complex symplectic. Since ℳ\mathcal{M} has no rel, for every equivalence class 𝒟\mathcal{D} of horizontal cylinders on (X,ω)(X,\omega) there is a tangent vector v𝒟v_{\mathcal{D}} which is nonzero on the core curve of every cylinder in 𝒟\mathcal{D} and which vanishes on the core curve of every other horizontal cylinder in (X,ω)(X,\omega). There is also the standard shear σ𝒟\sigma_{\mathcal{D}} which is supported on 𝒟\mathcal{D}. Notice that

B:={σ𝒟,v𝒟: 𝒟 a horizontal equivalence class on (X,ω) }B:=\{\sigma_{\mathcal{D}},v_{\mathcal{D}}:\text{ $\mathcal{D}$ a horizontal equivalence class on $(X,\omega)$ }\}

is a basis of the tangent space of ℳ\mathcal{M} at (X,ω)(X,\omega). Let VV be an open connected neighborhood of (X,ω)(X,\omega) on which all horizontal cylinders and all vectors in BB remain well-defined tangent directions.

Lemma 6.5.

Suppose that (X,ω)(X,\omega) is a horizontally periodic translation surface in ℳ\mathcal{M} with twist space and cylinder preserving space coinciding. Suppose that 𝒞\mathcal{C} is an ℳ\mathcal{M}-equivalence class of horizontal cylinders on (X,ω)(X,\omega) that contains exactly two cylinders. Let VV be as above. If the cylinders in 𝒞\mathcal{C} are simple for some (Y,η)∈V(Y,\eta)\in V, then the cylinders in 𝒞\mathcal{C} are similar on (Y,η)(Y,\eta).

Proof.

Let 𝒞={C1,C2}\mathcal{C}=\{C_{1},C_{2}\} and suppose to a contradiction that they are not similar on (Y,η)(Y,\eta). Since they are not similar, on (Y,η)(Y,\eta) use the standard shear to shear 𝒞\mathcal{C} (which is still an equivalence class on (Y,η)(Y,\eta) by Lemma 6.4) so that one cylinder, say C1C_{1}, has a vertical saddle connection vv, but C2C_{2} does not. Let (Y,η)(Y,\eta) now denote this new surface.

Apply the standard deformation to 𝒞\mathcal{C} to send the period of vv to zero while only altering imaginary parts of periods. Let (Z,ζ)(Z,\zeta) be the resulting boundary translation surface. Since only the height of one simple cylinder vanished, (Z,ζ)(Z,\zeta) is connected. Let 𝒩\mathcal{N} be the largest affine invariant submanifold in the boundary of ℳ\mathcal{M} containing (Z,ζ)(Z,\zeta) (the boundary is defined in Mirzakhani-Wright [MW17]).

Let {𝒟i}i=1r\{\mathcal{D}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{r} be the horizontal ℳ\mathcal{M}-equivalence classes on (X,ω)(X,\omega). Suppose too that 𝒟1=𝒞\mathcal{D}_{1}=\mathcal{C}. In the basis {σ𝒟i,v𝒟i}i=1r\{\sigma_{\mathcal{D}_{i}},v_{\mathcal{D}_{i}}\}_{i=1}^{r} of the tangent space of ℳ\mathcal{M} at (Y,η)(Y,\eta) the only deformations that fail to fix 𝒞\mathcal{C} are σ𝒞\sigma_{\mathcal{C}} and v𝒞v_{\mathcal{C}}. By Mirzakhani-Wright [MW17, Theorem 2.7], the span of {σ𝒟i,v𝒟i}i=2r∪{v𝒞}\{\sigma_{\mathcal{D}_{i}},v_{\mathcal{D}_{i}}\}_{i=2}^{r}\cup\{v_{\mathcal{C}}\} injects into the tangent space of 𝒩\mathcal{N} at (Z,ζ)(Z,\zeta). Since all cylinders in ⋃i≠1𝒟i\bigcup_{i\neq 1}\mathcal{D}_{i} persist (and are disjoint) on (Z,ζ)(Z,\zeta), we observe that the image of v𝒟iv_{\mathcal{D}_{i}} on (Z,ζ)(Z,\zeta) (for i≠1i\neq 1) causes cylinders in 𝒟i\mathcal{D}_{i} to have the period of their core curves change while fixing the periods of the core curves of all other cylinders in ⋃i≠1𝒟i\bigcup_{i\neq 1}\mathcal{D}_{i}.

Recall that the rank of 𝒩\mathcal{N} is the maximum dimension of the ℚ\mathbb{Q} linear span of the periods of the core curves of a collection of disjoint cylinders on translation surfaces in 𝒩\mathcal{N}. Therefore, we see that the rank of 𝒩\mathcal{N} is at least r−1r-1. By Mirzakhani-Wright [MW17, Corollary 2.8] the rank of 𝒩\mathcal{N} is strictly smaller than the rank of ℳ\mathcal{M} so the rank of 𝒩\mathcal{N} is exactly r−1r-1. Therefore, {σ𝒟i,v𝒟i}i=2r\{\sigma_{\mathcal{D}_{i}},v_{\mathcal{D}_{i}}\}_{i=2}^{r} forms a basis of the projection of T(Z,ζ)​𝒩T_{(Z,\zeta)}\mathcal{N} to absolute cohomology, taken as a complex vector space.

There is a vector vv in the span of {σ𝒟i,v𝒟i}i=2r\{\sigma_{\mathcal{D}_{i}},v_{\mathcal{D}_{i}}\}_{i=2}^{r} so that v𝒞−vv_{\mathcal{C}}-v is rel. Let γ\gamma be the image of the core curve of C2C_{2} on (Z,ζ)(Z,\zeta). Since C2C_{2} did not contain a vertical saddle connection, γ\gamma remains an absolute homology class on (Z,ζ)(Z,\zeta). Moreover, vv preserves γ\gamma while v𝒞v_{\mathcal{C}} changes its period. Therefore, v𝒞−vv_{\mathcal{C}}-v changes the period of an absolute homology class and hence cannot be rel, which is a contradiction. ∎

Lemma 6.6 (Similar Cylinder Lemma).

Suppose that ℳ\mathcal{M} is an affine invariant submanifold that has no rel. Let (Y,η)(Y,\eta) be a translation surface with two simple cylinders C1C_{1} and C2C_{2} that form an equivalence class 𝒞\mathcal{C}. It follows that C1C_{1} and C2C_{2} are similar.

Proof.

As explained in the proof of the cylinder deformation theorem Wright [Wri15, Theorem 1.1], by appealing to Smillie-Weiss [SW10], it is possible to use horocycle flow in the horizontal direction and arbitrarily small perturbations to start with the surface (Y,η)(Y,\eta) with two simple horizontal cylinders in 𝒞\mathcal{C} and end with a surface (X,ω)(X,\omega) in ℳ\mathcal{M} that is horizontally periodic with the twist space coinciding with the cylinder preserving space and so that C1C_{1} and C2C_{2} persist on (X,ω)(X,\omega) as simple cylinders congruent to the corresponding cylinders on (Y,η)(Y,\eta). Since the process only involves hororcycle flow and arbitrarily small perturbations, we have by Lemma 6.4 that 𝒞\mathcal{C} remains an equivalence class on (X,ω)(X,\omega). By Lemma 6.5, C1C_{1} and C2C_{2} are similar. ∎

7. Proof of Theorem 2 - Classification of Higher Rank Nonarithmetic Affine Invariant Submanifolds in ℋ⁡(6)\mathcal{H}(6)

Thoughout this section we will make the following assumption:

Assumption 7.1.

ℳ\mathcal{M} is a rank two nonarithmetic affine invariant submanifold in ℋ⁡(6)\mathcal{H}(6)

Our goal is to show that there is only one such affine invariant submanifold.

Lemma 7.2.

There is a vertically and horizontally periodic translation surface in ℳ\mathcal{M} with two vertical and horizontal equivalence classes {𝒞1,𝒞2}\{\mathcal{C}_{1},\mathcal{C}_{2}\} and {𝒱1,𝒱2}\{\mathcal{V}_{1},\mathcal{V}_{2}\} respectively so that the following hold:

  1. (1)

    𝒱2\mathcal{V}_{2} is contained in 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2}

  2. (2)

    𝒞1\mathcal{C}_{1} is contained in 𝒱1\mathcal{V}_{1}

  3. (3)

    𝒞1\mathcal{C}_{1} contains a vertical saddle connection

  4. (4)

    𝒱2\mathcal{V}_{2} contains a horizontal saddle connection

Proof.

By the prototype lemma in Apisa [Apib], there is a translation surface (X0,ω0)(X_{0},\omega_{0}) that satisfies the first two hypotheses. Use the standard shear to shear 𝒞1\mathcal{C}_{1} so that it contains a vertical saddle connection and call the resulting translation surface (X1,ω1)(X_{1},\omega_{1}).

Vertically collapse 𝒞1\mathcal{C}_{1} (i.e. apply the standard shear to send the period of the vertical saddle connection in 𝒞1\mathcal{C}_{1} to zero while only changing imaginary parts of periods). Each component of the boundary translation surface contains 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2}, which was not affected by the degeneration. In particular, since 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2} contains 𝒱2\mathcal{V}_{2}, each component of the boundary translation surface contains a vertical cylinder. Since each component of the boundary translation surface is contained in a rank one orbit closure by Mirzakhani-Wright [MW17, Corollary 2.8] it is completely vertically periodic by Wright [Wri15, Theorem 1.5]. Since 𝒞1\mathcal{C}_{1} was vertically collapsed, it follows that (X1,ω1)(X_{1},\omega_{1}) remains vertically and horizontally periodic and satisfies properties 11 through 33.

Now use the standard shear to shear 𝒱2\mathcal{V}_{2} so that it contains a horizontal saddle connection and call the resulting surface (X2,ω2)(X_{2},\omega_{2}). The argument just given shows that (X2,ω2)(X_{2},\omega_{2}) is the desired surface. ∎

Remark 7.3.

By Wright [Wri15, Theorem 1.9], since ℳ\mathcal{M} is nonarithmetic each equivalence class must contain at least two cylinders. Since a translation surface in ℋ⁡(6)\mathcal{H}(6) has at most four cylinders in a given direction, each equivalence class contains exactly two cylinders.

Assumption 7.4.

Let (X,ω)(X,\omega) be a surface in ℳ\mathcal{M} satisfying the conclusion of Lemma 7.2.

Definition 7.5.

“Collapsing 𝒞1\mathcal{C}_{1}” will mean applying the standard shear to 𝒞1\mathcal{C}_{1} to only alter the imaginary parts of periods while sending the period of the vertical saddle connection contained in 𝒞1\mathcal{C}_{1} to zero. We will use the phrase “collapsing 𝒱2\mathcal{V}_{2}” analogously.

Lemma 7.6.

Collapsing 𝒱2\mathcal{V}_{2} produces a boundary translation surface where each component belongs to a rank one rel one orbit closure in the boundary of ℳ\mathcal{M}. The rel deformation is a linear combination of the images on the boundary of the standard shears of the horizontal equivalence classes on (X,ω)(X,\omega). By symmetry of hypotheses, the same holds when 𝒞1\mathcal{C}_{1} is collapsed.

Proof.

Let (Z,ζ)(Z,\zeta) be any component of the surface obtained by collapsing 𝒞1\mathcal{C}_{1} and let 𝒩\mathcal{N} be the largest orbit closure in the boundary of ℳ\mathcal{M} containing (Z,ζ)(Z,\zeta). Since (Z,ζ)(Z,\zeta) contains a vertical cylinder that previously belonged to 𝒱1\mathcal{V}_{1} - which intersected 𝒞1\mathcal{C}_{1} and 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2} on (X,ω)(X,\omega) - it follows that 𝒩\mathcal{N} contains tangent vectors, say σ1\sigma_{1} and σ2\sigma_{2}, coming from the standard shears on 𝒞1\mathcal{C}_{1} and 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2}.

By Mirzakhani-Wright [MW17, Corollary 2.8], 𝒩\mathcal{N} is rank one, meaning that the projection of T(Z,ζ)​𝒩T_{(Z,\zeta)}\mathcal{N} to absolute cohomology is a two complex-dimensional symplectic vector space. Since σ1\sigma_{1} and σ2\sigma_{2} are supported on disjoint cylinders, they have intersection number zero. Therefore, there is a constant cc so that c​σ1c\sigma_{1} and σ2\sigma_{2} project to the same absolute cohomology class. In particular, this means that σ1−c​σ2\sigma_{1}-c\sigma_{2} is a nonzero relative deformation. Consequently, 𝒩\mathcal{N} has rel at least one, and since 𝒩\mathcal{N} is three complex-dimensional 𝒩\mathcal{N} must be a rank one rel one orbit closure as desired. ∎

Lemma 7.7.

There is a cylinder in 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2} that has a horizontal saddle connection attaching its top boundary to its bottom boundary. This saddle connection is necessarily contained in 𝒱2\mathcal{V}_{2}. By symmetry, the analogous statement holds for 𝒱1\mathcal{V}_{1}.

Proof.

Suppose not to a contradiction. Let C2C_{2} and C2′C_{2}^{\prime} be the two cylinders in 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2}. Since the cylinders in 𝒱2\mathcal{V}_{2} are contained in 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2}, each cylinder in 𝒱2\mathcal{V}_{2} intersects the core curve of C2C_{2} and C2′C_{2}^{\prime} an equal number of times (since there are no saddle connections joining the top and bottom of a cylinder in 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2}). This means that the ratio of the lengths of the core curves of the cylinders in 𝒱2\mathcal{V}_{2} is an integer or the reciprocal of an integer. In particular, by Wright [Wri15, Theorem 1.9] ℳ\mathcal{M} is arithmetic, which contradicts Assumption 7.1 that ℳ\mathcal{M} is nonarithmetic.

It remains to show that 𝒱2\mathcal{V}_{2} contains the saddle connection. Collapsing 𝒱2\mathcal{V}_{2} creates a boundary translation surface that has rel by supported on its horizontal cylinders by Lemma 7.6. This is not possible if a horizontal cylinder in 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2} has a horizontal saddle connection joining its top and bottom. Therefore, 𝒱2\mathcal{V}_{2} must contain any such saddle connection. ∎

Definition 7.8.

If two cylinders are connected by a saddle connection, then we will say that they are adjacent. If they are connected by a saddle connection on their top and bottom boundaries, then we will say that they are two-sided adjacent.

Definition 7.9.

Define ℳ0\mathcal{M}_{0} to be the smallest affine invariant submanifold containing the translation surfaces in Figure 24 with λ\lambda equal to the golden ratio, opposite sides identified, all angles integer multiples of π2\frac{\pi}{2}, and xix_{i} and yiy_{i} arbitrary positive real numbers for i=1,2i=1,2.

Lemma 7.10.

If collapsing 𝒱2\mathcal{V}_{2} disconnects the surface, then ℳ=ℳ0\mathcal{M}=\mathcal{M}_{0}.

Proof.

Let (Y,η)(Y,\eta) be the disconnected boundary translation surface that arises from collapsing 𝒱2\mathcal{V}_{2}. Each component of (Y,η)(Y,\eta) contains at least one cylinder from 𝒱1\mathcal{V}_{1}. Since 𝒱1\mathcal{V}_{1} contains exactly two cylinders and (Y,η)(Y,\eta) has at least two components, it follows that (Y,η)(Y,\eta) has exactly two components, each of which contains exactly one cylinder from 𝒱1\mathcal{V}_{1}. This implies that the two cylinders in 𝒱1\mathcal{V}_{1} share no boundary on (X,ω)(X,\omega). In particular, this means that the two cylinders in 𝒱1\mathcal{V}_{1} are disjoint and, in fact, never intersect the same horizontal cylinder.

Since each component of (Y,η)(Y,\eta) must contain a cylinder from 𝒞1\mathcal{C}_{1} we notice that the cylinders from 𝒞1\mathcal{C}_{1} must also be disjoint and adjacent to a unique cylinder in 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2}. If there is not a cylinder in 𝒱2\mathcal{V}_{2} that passes through both cylinders in 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2}, then (X,ω)(X,\omega) would be disconnected. It follows that the cylinders in 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2} are two-sided adjacent. Since the cylinders in 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2} are no longer adjacent on (Y,η)(Y,\eta) it follows that 𝒱2\mathcal{V}_{2} contains the three horizontal saddle connections that join the top boundary of a cylinder in 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2} to the bottom boundary of another (one saddle connection comes from Lemma 7.7 and the other two come since the two cylinders in 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2} are two-sided adjacent on (X,ω)(X,\omega), but not on (Y,η)(Y,\eta)).

Since there are seven horizontal saddle connections on (X,ω)(X,\omega), the cylinders in 𝒞1\mathcal{C}_{1} are disjoint and simple. The similar cylinder lemma (Lemma 6.6) implies that the two cylinders in 𝒞1\mathcal{C}_{1} are similar and hence both contain a vertical saddle connection. Moreover, the core curve of each cylinder in 𝒱1\mathcal{V}_{1} must intersect the core curve of a cylinder in 𝒞1\mathcal{C}_{1} either zero or one time, see the left subfigure of Figure 22.

By applying the standard shear to shear 𝒞1\mathcal{C}_{1} and 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2} in opposite directions as in Figure 22, we may perturb (X,ω)(X,\omega) in a way to make the cylinders in 𝒱1\mathcal{V}_{1} are simple. The simple cylinder lemma (Lemma 6.6) implies that the cylinders in 𝒱1\mathcal{V}_{1} are similar on the perturbed surface. Since the two cylinders in 𝒞1\mathcal{C}_{1} were similar too we see that the cylinder proportion theorem [NW14, Proposition 3.2] implies that the two cylinders in 𝒱1\mathcal{V}_{1} are also similar on (X,ω)(X,\omega). We can now write down the surface explicitly; it is the translation surface shown in Figure 23 or its mirror image about the vertical.

In Figure 23, opposite sides are identified unless labelled with a,b,σ⁡(a)a,b,\sigma(a), or σ⁡(b)\sigma(b). We let σ\sigma be a permutation of {a,b}\{a,b\} that indicates how sides are identified. All other labels indicate lengths with x1,x2,y1,y2x_{1},x_{2},y_{1},y_{2}, and λ\lambda being real numbers. By the cylinder proportion theorem [NW14, Proposition 3.2], λ>1\lambda>1.

If σ⁡(b)=a\sigma(b)=a then we see that one cylinder in 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2} contains a diagonal cylinder that does not intersect 𝒱1\mathcal{V}_{1}. Since the other cylinder in 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2} cannot contain such a cylinder this violates the cylinder proportion theorem [NW14, Proposition 3.2] . Therefore, σ⁡(a)=a\sigma(a)=a and σ⁡(b)=b\sigma(b)=b. It follows that (X,ω)(X,\omega) is the translation surface shown in Figure 24 or its mirror image about the vertical (for some choice of x1,x2,y1x_{1},x_{2},y_{1}, and y2y_{2}). The fact that ℳ\mathcal{M} contains all surfaces in Figure 24 for arbitrary positive real xix_{i} and yiy_{i} (i=1,2i=1,2) follows from the fact that the standard shears in 𝒞i\mathcal{C}_{i} and 𝒱i\mathcal{V}_{i} remain in ℳ\mathcal{M}; this holds by the cylinder deformation theorem [Wri15, Theorem 1.1].

Collapsing 𝒞1\mathcal{C}_{1} produces a boundary translation surface (Z,ζ)(Z,\zeta) in ℋ⁡(1,1,0)\mathcal{H}(1,1,0). By Lemma 7.6, (Z,ζ)(Z,\zeta) is contained in a three dimensional orbit closure 𝒩\mathcal{N} in the boundary of ℳ\mathcal{M} and the relative deformation alters all four vertical cylinders. Therefore, 𝒩\mathcal{N} is a three-dimensional nonarithmetic eigenform locus in ℋ⁡(1,1)\mathcal{H}(1,1) with a non-Weierstrass periodic point marked. By Theorem 1, 𝒩\mathcal{N} is the golden eigenform locus with a golden point marked and since λ>1\lambda>1, λ\lambda is the golden ratio.

The affine invariant submanifold ℳ0\mathcal{M}_{0} is defined precisely as the smallest affine invariant submanifold containing the translation surfaces in Figure 24 with λ\lambda the golden ratio and xix_{i} and yiy_{i} arbitrary positive real numbers for i=1,2i=1,2. The four cohomology classes that correspond to changing x1x_{1}, x2x_{2}, y1y_{1}, or y2y_{2} span a four complex-dimensional subspace of absolute cohomology. Since the tangent space of ℳ\mathcal{M} is four complex-dimensional, it follows that these cohomology classes span the tangent space to ℳ\mathcal{M} at (X,ω)(X,\omega). Since these classes are contained in ℳ0\mathcal{M}_{0}, it follows that ℳ\mathcal{M} coincides with ℳ0\mathcal{M}_{0}.

Recall finally that we showed that (X,ω)(X,\omega) is the translation surface shown in Figure 24 up to taking a mirror image in the vertical. However, the mirror image of the translation surface in Figure 24 about the vertical is identical to its rotation by π\pi and hence in this case ℳ\mathcal{M} is still equal to ℳ0\mathcal{M}_{0}. ∎

In light of Lemma 7.10 we make the following assumption:

Assumption 7.11.

The surface (X,ω)(X,\omega) is not disconnected when 𝒞1\mathcal{C}_{1} or 𝒱2\mathcal{V}_{2} collapses.

Recall that given a horizontally periodic surface the cylinder graph is the directed graph whose vertices are cylinders and that has a directed edge from cylinder AA to cylinder BB if the top boundary of AA borders the bottom boundary of BB. The cylinder graph is always strongly connected.

Lemma 7.12.

There are at most three horizontal saddle connections connecting cylinders in 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2} to cylinders in 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2}.

Proof.

Suppose not to a contradiction. For a horizontally periodic translation surface in ℋ⁡(6)\mathcal{H}(6) there are seven horizontal saddle connections and at least four connect cylinders in 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2} to other cylinders in 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2}. Since only three saddle connections remain and since the cylinder graph must be strongly connected, there must be a directed edge from a cylinder in 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2} to a cylinder C1∈𝒞1C_{1}\in\mathcal{C}_{1}; a directed edge from C1C_{1} to a distinct cylinder C1′∈𝒞1C_{1}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{C}_{1}; and a directed edge from C1′C_{1}^{\prime} to some cylinder in 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2}. However, this configuration implies that there is a marked point on the boundary of C1C_{1} and C1′C_{1}^{\prime}, which is not possible. Therefore, we have a contradiction. ∎

Lemma 7.13.

There are two horizontal saddle connections contained in 𝒱2\mathcal{V}_{2}. By symmetry, 𝒞1\mathcal{C}_{1} contains two vertical saddle connections.

Proof.

We divide the proposition into two cases.

Case 1: 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2} is not two-sided adjacent

If 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2} is not two-sided adjacent, then each cylinder in 𝒱2\mathcal{V}_{2} is contained in a unique cylinder in 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2}.

If 𝒱2\mathcal{V}_{2} contains three horizontal saddle connections, then the (horizontal) cylinder graph must contain three loops - directed edges that begin and end at the same vertex - based at vertices in 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2}. Ignoring these edges we see that the remaining four edges must form a strongly connected directed graph on the four vertices. This is only possible if these edges form a directed four-cycle. This implies that the two cylinders in 𝒞1\mathcal{C}_{1} are homologous, which is impossible in a minimal stratum. Alternatively, the two cylinders in 𝒞1\mathcal{C}_{1} must have core curves of identical length, which yields the contradiction that ℳ\mathcal{M} is arithmetic by Wright [Wri15, Theorem 1.9].

Therefore, 𝒱2\mathcal{V}_{2} must contain at most two horizontal saddle connections by Lemma 7.12. Since the two cylinders in 𝒱2\mathcal{V}_{2} are simple and disjoint they must be similar by the similar cylinder lemma (Lemma 6.6). Since 𝒱2\mathcal{V}_{2} contains at least one horizontal saddle connection by Assumption 7.4, it must contain exactly two horizontal saddle connections.

Case 2: 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2} is two-sided adjacent

By Assumption 7.4, 𝒱2\mathcal{V}_{2} contains at least one horizontal saddle connection and by Lemma 7.12 it contains at most three.

If 𝒱2\mathcal{V}_{2} contains exactly one, then collapsing 𝒱2\mathcal{V}_{2} leaves 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2} two-sided adjacent. However, by Lemma 7.6 the boundary translation surface formed by collapsing 𝒱2\mathcal{V}_{2} has a rel deformation that is a linear combination of the standard shears on the horizontal cylinders. However, there is a closed curve γ\gamma that is contained in 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2} (since 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2} is two-sided adjacent) and whose period is changed by standard shear on 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2}. This contradicts the definition of a rel deformation.

If 𝒱2\mathcal{V}_{2} contains exactly three horizontal saddle connections, then collapsing it produces a connected (by Assumption 7.11) translation surface with four horizontal cylinders. The horizontal cylinder graph contains four vertices and four edges and therefore is a directed four-cycle. This corresponds to a horizontally periodic flat torus with four marked points. On the boundary translation surface all cylinders have core curves of equal length. Since the lengths of the core curves of the cylinders in 𝒞1\mathcal{C}_{1} were unaffected by collapsing 𝒱2\mathcal{V}_{2}, it follows that they had identical lengths on (X,ω)(X,\omega) and hence ℳ\mathcal{M} is arithmetic by Wright [Wri15, Theorem 1.9]; contradicting Assumption 7.1 which states that ℳ\mathcal{M} is nonarithmetic. Therefore, 𝒱2\mathcal{V}_{2} contains exactly two horizontal saddle connections.

∎

Lemma 7.14.

Collapsing 𝒱2\mathcal{V}_{2} yields a surface in the golden eigenform locus with the golden point marked. The same statement holds for 𝒞1\mathcal{C}_{1} by symmetry.

Proof.

Collapse 𝒱2\mathcal{V}_{2} and let (Y,η)(Y,\eta) be the genus gg boundary translation surface. Let 𝒩\mathcal{N} be the largest connected orbit closure in the boundary of ℳ\mathcal{M} containing (Y,η)(Y,\eta). By Assumption 7.11, (Y,η)(Y,\eta) is connected and contains four horizontal cylinders. By Lemma 7.13 it contains five horizontal saddle connections. By Lemma 7.6, a linear combination of the standard shears of the two horizontal equivalence classes of cylinders on (X,ω)(X,\omega) becomes a rel deformation on (Y,η)(Y,\eta). In particular, this means that the number of zeros and marked points, ss, on (Y,η)(Y,\eta) is at least two.

The horizontal saddle connections on a horizontally periodic translation surface is 2​g+s−22g+s-2, which in this case is five. Since s≥2s\geq 2, we have that g=1,2g=1,2. If g=1g=1, then all horizontal cylinders have core curves of equal length. In particular, the cylinders in 𝒞1\mathcal{C}_{1} on (X,ω)(X,\omega) have core curves of equal length, which implies that ℳ\mathcal{M} is arithmetic by Wright [Wri15, Theorem 1.9]. This contradicts Assumption 7.1. So g=2g=2 and s=3s=3.

Since the lengths of the core curves of the cylinders in 𝒞1\mathcal{C}_{1} is unchanged as 𝒱2\mathcal{V}_{2} collapses, the ratio of these lengths remains nonarithmetic on (Y,η)(Y,\eta). Since 𝒩\mathcal{N} is a rank one rel one orbit closure by Lemma 7.6, 𝒩\mathcal{N} is nonarithmetic and belongs to either ℋ⁡(2,0,0)\mathcal{H}(2,0,0) or ℋ⁡(1,1,0)\mathcal{H}(1,1,0). Since 𝒩\mathcal{N} is nonarithmetic, the projection that sends 𝒩\mathcal{N} to ℋ⁡(2)\mathcal{H}(2) or ℋ⁡(1,1)\mathcal{H}(1,1) by forgetting marked points is contained in a nonarithmetic eigenform locus 𝒩′\mathcal{N}^{\prime}.

Suppose to a contradiction that (Y,η)(Y,\eta) belongs to ℋ⁡(2,0,0)\mathcal{H}(2,0,0). Since 𝒩\mathcal{N} is nonarithmetic, the projection to ℋ⁡(2)\mathcal{H}(2) that forgets marked points has as its image a nonarithmetic Teichmüller curve. By Apisa-Wright [AW17, Theorem 1.3], the two marked points are either (1) a periodic point and an unconstrained point, or (2) two points exchanged by the hyperelliptic involution. In the first case, the relative deformation is moving the unconstrained point (which involves altering two cylinders on (Y,η)(Y,\eta)) while fixing the rest of the surface. In the second, the relative deformation is moving one marked point and having its image under the hyperelliptic involution move in the opposite direction (which involves altering three cylinders on (Y,η)(Y,\eta) since a marked point and its image under the hyperelliptic involution are contained in the same horizontal cylinder on the unmarked surface) while fixing the rest of the surface. However, the relative deformation is a linear combination of the two standard shears of the horizontal equivalence classes on (X,ω)(X,\omega) and hence must involve all four horizontal cylinders. This is a contradiction.

Therefore, (Y,η)(Y,\eta) belongs to ℋ⁡(1,1,0)\mathcal{H}(1,1,0). As before, 𝒩′\mathcal{N}^{\prime} is either the decagon locus or a nonarithmetic eigenform locus. If 𝒩′\mathcal{N}^{\prime} is the decagon locus, then the marked point is unconstrained and the relative deformation is simply moving the unconstrained point around the surface. This deformation involves at most two cylinders, which is a contradiction as before.

Suppose now that 𝒩′\mathcal{N}^{\prime} is a nonarithmetic eigenform locus in ℋ⁡(1,1)\mathcal{H}(1,1). The marked point must be a periodic point. If the marked point is a Weierstrass point, then there are two congruent cylinders C1C_{1} and C2C_{2} on (Y,η)(Y,\eta) that are generically congruent on 𝒩\mathcal{N}. Since these cylinders have generically equal heights in 𝒩\mathcal{N} they must be the image of an equivalence class of horizontal cylinders on (X,ω)(X,\omega). However, since they have generically equal lengths of core curves, ℳ\mathcal{M} is arithmetic by Wright [Wri15, Theorem 1.9], which contradicts Assumption 7.1. Therefore, the marked point is a periodic point that is not a Weierstrass point. This implies that 𝒩′\mathcal{N}^{\prime} contains surfaces in the golden eigenform locus with the golden point marked.

∎

Once 𝒱2\mathcal{V}_{2} is collapsed, Lemma 7.14 implies that the resulting boundary translation surface is the one shown in Figure 25 up to rotation by π\pi. The figure is only accurate in how it illustrates how horizontal cylinders are attached to one another. In Figure 25, opposite sides are identified, and the cylinders in each equivalence class are labelled.

Lemma 7.15.

Either 𝒞1\mathcal{C}_{1} or 𝒱2\mathcal{V}_{2} contains two disjoint simple cylinders.

Proof.

Let (Y,η)(Y,\eta) be the translation surface obtained by collapsing 𝒱2\mathcal{V}_{2} on (X,ω)(X,\omega). We divide the proof into two cases.

Case 1: The two cylinders in 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2} are adjacent to each other

If the two cylinders in 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2} are two-sided adjacent, then there are at least three horizontal saddle connections on the boundary of 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2} that connects a cylinder in 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2} to a cylinder in 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2} (there are two such saddle connections joining the two distinct cylinders and then one more joining a cylinder in 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2} to itself by Lemma 7.7). If the two cylinders are one-sided adjacent then there are still at least three horizontal saddle connections on their boundary (there is one saddle connection joining the two distinct cylinders and then two saddle connections in 𝒱2\mathcal{V}_{2} that connect the boundary of a cylinder to itself). By Lemma 7.12, there are exactly three horizontal saddle connections on the boundary of 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2}. By Lemma 7.13, there are only two horizontal saddle connections contained in 𝒱2\mathcal{V}_{2}. Therefore, the two cylinders in 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2} remain adjacent on the boundary translation surface (Y,η)(Y,\eta). In particular, (Y,η)(Y,\eta) must be the rightmost figure in Figure 25. We see that the two cylinders in 𝒞1\mathcal{C}_{1} are disjoint and simple on (X,ω)(X,\omega).

Case 2: The two cylinders in 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2} are not adjacent to each other

As we proved in Lemma 7.13 Case 1, if the two cylinders in 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2} are not adjacent, then there are exactly two horizontal saddle connections that connect two cylinders in 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2}. This shows that 𝒱2\mathcal{V}_{2} contains two disjoint simple cylinders.

∎

Without loss of generality, perhaps after rotating (X,ω)(X,\omega) by π2\frac{\pi}{2} we make the following assumption:

Assumption 7.16.

Assume that 𝒱2\mathcal{V}_{2} contains two disjoint simple cylinders

This is the first assumption that we have made that is not symmetric in how it treats the horizontal and vertical direction.

Proof of Theorem 2.

We will begin by showing that ℳ\mathcal{M} coincides with ℳ0\mathcal{M}_{0}. By Lemma 7.14 the boundary translation surface (Y,η)(Y,\eta) formed by collapsing 𝒱2\mathcal{V}_{2} is the golden eigenform locus with the golden point marked (see Figure 25, which is only an accurate up to rotation by π\pi, and only represents horizontal cylinders adjacency). Since 𝒱2\mathcal{V}_{2} contains two disjoint simple cylinders, these cylinders become vertical saddle connections on (Y,η)(Y,\eta) that are contained in 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2}

Case 1: The cylinders in 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2} are not adjacent

This implies that (Y,η)(Y,\eta) is the rightmost figure in Figure 25. Since both cylinders in 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2} on (Y,η)(Y,\eta) contain a vertical saddle connection we see that both cylinders in 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2} on (Y,η)(Y,\eta) are as drawn in Figure 25. Moreover, apply the standard shear to the cylinders in 𝒞1\mathcal{C}_{1} so that (Y,η)(Y,\eta) is, after deforming the cylinders in 𝒞1\mathcal{C}_{1}, exactly as drawn in Figure 26. The two vertical saddle connections coming from the image of the core curves of the cylinders in 𝒱2\mathcal{V}_{2} are labelled s1s_{1} and s2s_{2}.

Opening up the collapsed simple cylinders shows us that the orbit closure contained the surface in Figure 27 up to rotation by π\pi. Opposite sides of the polygon are identified and labels indicate length where xix_{i} and yiy_{i} are arbitrary positive real numbers for i=1,2i=1,2, and ϕ\phi is the golden ratio.

This surface is the one in Figure 24 rotated by π2\frac{\pi}{2} and so the orbit closure of ℳ\mathcal{M} is ℳ0\mathcal{M}_{0} as desired.

Case 2: The cylinders in 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2} are adjacent

As we argued in Lemma 7.15 Case 1, after 𝒱2\mathcal{V}_{2} collapses we must be in the leftmost figure of Figure 25. The simple cylinders in 𝒱2\mathcal{V}_{2} are now two vertical saddle connections in the cylinders labeled 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2}. By Assumption 7.4, 𝒞1\mathcal{C}_{1} contains a vertical saddle connection. Since 𝒞1\mathcal{C}_{1} contains two disjoint simple cylinders they must be similar by the similar cylinder lemma (Lemma 6.6) and so both contain a vertical saddle connection. Therefore, the surface drawn in Figure 25 is correct up to determining how the cylinders in 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2} may be sheared to contain two vertical saddle connections. The four options are shown in Figure 28.

Subcase 2a: Ruling out the leftmost figure in Figure 28

The first figure has two possible pairs of vertical saddle connections, either {s1,s2}\{s_{1},s_{2}\} or {s1′,s2}\{s_{1}^{\prime},s_{2}\}. The pair of cylinders {s1,s1′}\{s_{1},s_{1}^{\prime}\} is not possible since this would imply that there is a cylinder in 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2} on (X,ω)(X,\omega) that does not intersect 𝒱2\mathcal{V}_{2}, which violates the cylinder proportion theorem [NW14, Proposition 3.2]. Opening up {s1,s2}\{s_{1},s_{2}\} into simple cylinders produces the translation surface in Figure 29. Opposite sides are identified and labels are lengths where ϕ\phi is the golden ratio and x,y,z,x,y,z, and ww are arbitrary positive real numbers. Opening up {s1′,s2}\{s_{1}^{\prime},s_{2}\} yields the surface in Figure 29 rotated by π2\frac{\pi}{2}.

Choose xx and ww so that ϕ​x<(ϕ−1)​w\phi x<(\phi-1)w. In Figure 30A, we identify two dashed saddle connections. We will apply the standard shear in 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2} so that these two saddle connections are vertical. Then we will apply the standard shear to preserve the real parts of all periods while sending the periods of these two saddle connections to zero. The dotted lines have been drawn in to keep track of where the zeros go in this degeneration. The result of the degeneration is shown in Figure 30B.

The surface (Y,η)(Y,\eta) in Figure 30B. belongs to ℋ⁡(2,0,0)\mathcal{H}(2,0,0) and the lengths of the edges are

|a|=ϕ​x|b|=(ϕ−1)​w−ϕ​x|c|=x|d|=w−x|a|=\phi x\quad|b|=(\phi-1)w-\phi x\quad|c|=x\quad|d|=w-x

Since ww and xx may be altered freely, as may the heights of the cylinders in 𝒞1\mathcal{C}_{1} we see that the boundary translation surface has orbit closure 𝒩\mathcal{N} of dimension at least three. By Mirzakhani-Wright [MW17, Corollary 2.8], 𝒩\mathcal{N} has dimension exactly equal to three. Since (Y,η)(Y,\eta) is a completely periodic surface whose horizontal cylinders have irrational ratio of lengths of core curves, (Y,η)(Y,\eta) is an eigenform of real multiplication. Therefore, the only periodic points are Weierstrass points. By Apisa-Wright [AW17, Theorem 1.3], the two marked points are either (1) a Weierstrass point and an unconstrained point, or (2) two points exchanged by the hyperelliptic involution. The two marked points are not exchanged by the hyperelliptic involution and neither is a Weierstrass point as long as |a|≠|b||a|\neq|b|, which is generically the case. Therefore, we have a contradiction.

Subcase 2b: The right two figures in Figure 28

Slicing the right two figures in Figure 28 along {s1,s2}\{s_{1},s_{2}\} and inserting a simple cylinder yields two figures that differ by a reflection across the vertical. Our argument will show that one and hence both resulting translation surfaces belong to ℳ0\mathcal{M}_{0}.

The surface we produce is the leftmost one in Figure 31. We may shear the cylinders in 𝒞1\mathcal{C}_{1} to produce the rightmost figure in Figure 31, which contains two equivalent cylinders 𝒱1′\mathcal{V}_{1}^{\prime} (outlined in dashed lines) that contain 𝒞1\mathcal{C}_{1} and two more equivalent cylinders 𝒱2′\mathcal{V}_{2}^{\prime} that are contained in 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2}. Notice that Assumption 7.4 and Assumption 7.11 holds for this surface with the cylinder groups 𝒞1,𝒞2,𝒱1′,\mathcal{C}_{1},\mathcal{C}_{2},\mathcal{V}_{1}^{\prime}, and 𝒱2′\mathcal{V}_{2}^{\prime}. We see too that 𝒞1\mathcal{C}_{1} contains two disjoint simple cylinders, which is Assumption 7.16. Since the two cylinders in 𝒱1\mathcal{V}_{1} are disjoint we are in Case 1 of this proof, which shows that the surface must belong to ℳ0\mathcal{M}_{0}, as desired.

Periodic Points in ℳ\mathcal{M}

Now we will establish the second half the claim in Theorem 2, namely that ℳ\mathcal{M} has no periodic points. Suppose to a contradiction that pp is a periodic point on the translation surface (Z,ζ)(Z,\zeta) shown in Figure 24. By Apisa-Wright [AW17, Lemma 7.1] (which is a cleaner statement of a result in Apisa [Apia]) if the marked point lies in the interior of a cylinder in 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2} then it is one of the solid points shown in Figure 32. If it lies in the interior of a cylinder in 𝒱1\mathcal{V}_{1} then it is an open dot shown in Figure 32.

Any point may be moved into the interior of either 𝒱1\mathcal{V}_{1} or 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2} by using the standard shear in a horizontal or vertical equivalence class to perform one complete Dehn twist in those cylinders. Using these Dehn twists we see that the bottom three points are all in the same GL⁡(2,ℝ)\GL(2,\mathbb{R}) orbit, as are the top three points. However, using the standard shear to perform one complete Dehn twist in the cylinders in 𝒱2\mathcal{V}_{2} we see that the two solid points in 𝒱2\mathcal{V}_{2} are sent to points that cannot be periodic points. Therefore, ℳ\mathcal{M} contains no periodic points.

∎
